items.body: In the digital era, it’s rare to encounter a project as ambitious as this: a triple-LP concept album available as a boxed set, including a book with a short story (in Italian) and 180 illustrations. Un Sequestro Lungo 10,000 Anni is the love child of Samuele Gottardello (Blak Saagan) and Iranian illustrator Majid Bita, the second in a series of Opale Editions by Maple Death Records and Canicola Edizioni. The concept is dystopian, the illustrations vibrant despite their dual tones, portraying a world overrun by monsters and monstrous humans, a savage police force keeping a terrified and often angry populace at bay. In one scene, a bus rushes headlong toward a gaping maw. The apartments are jammed and often infested; Big Brother is everywhere, sharing the sky with the invading beasts. Helicopters roar and crash outside, while some citizens curl into balls and others smoke cigarettes, impassively observing the carnage. An informant uses a dial-up phone; a cleric mourns a fallen world. Angels and devils abound. Yet even amid the flames, there is room for art: writers and illustrators are hard at work, chronicling the chaos. The book’s final sentence: “Start dreaming again.” Given the artist’s background, it’s impossible to ignore the parallels with the current devestation in Iran: set upon from every angle, the populace is at the mercy of bombs from above and repression from below. And yet, this stark combination of dangers can rear its ugly head in any nation. While it’s tempting to think of the album as a dystopian vision (thanks to the presence of skyscraper-tall monsters), its visual metaphors can be applied to the present day. The rough translation: A 10,000 Year Long Kidnapping. Blak Saagan follows first a trajectory, and then an arc. The album begins with electronic music that segues gently into an ambient phase before toppling into rock and jazz and returning to the electronic. A few tracks contain vocals, but an entire LP side worth of material passes before the first words appear. An affection for 80s synth permeates the electronic pieces, conjuring associations with horror films; but while opener “The Blak Fire” is nearly industrial, the closer is as bright as the hopeful denouement. The early electronic pieces are metallic, propulsive and exciting, scoring what might be the initial invasion or the conflict already in progress; there will be time to slow down later, as people choose between the classic options: run, hide, die. “Everything will be swept away,” sings Julinko. Guitars surge like growling behemoths; drums pound like wide Kaiju feet. But by “Henran” (“Bewildered”), it all slows to a quiet boil, saxophone swelling as it struggles to take in a series of incomprehensible vistas. Time begins to distend; four of the final six tracks stretch past the ten minute mark. After the end, there is no more need for watches. The industrial timbres return in “FRREPa (featuring Liz Van Der Nüll)” ~ the sound of resistance re-awakening. The album’s shortest piece at 2:41, it packs the most powerful punch. At the beginning of the next piece, one can hear sirens and the sounds of street protest; the populace has awakened, and the revolution has begun. Midway through the piece, the BPMs increase along with the confidence of the movement. “Disintegrazione” offers a final pause for reflection before the completion of the arc, representing restoration. Such things have happened in history, which means they can happen again; but as this album warns, things may get a whole lot worse before they begin to improve. (Richard Allen)

Then we go down to Salvador da Bahia with “O Mundo Dá Voltas Dando Voltas Pelo Mundo”, reinterpretations of BaianaSystem‘s repertoire by producers from around the glove. items.body: Review by canadianeurysm — Where do I begin with The Whirlwind. Possibly the longest Epic ever created by a strong lineup. Everything about the people behind thispiece would suggest it would be outstanding.Mike Portnoy, Ronie Stolt, Pet Trewavas, and Neal Morse (More on the last member later).The song has great pace, and unlike a lot of modern prog it doesn't fall into sounding like a cloneof one of the heavy hitters of the genre (ELP, Yes, Genesis, King Crimson, etc.) - A lot of"smaller" prog bands draw a ton of inspiration from these guys and end up just sounding like a sidegrade. But not Transatlantic (and probably because individually these artists are from big bandsthemselves), there's certainly parallels with some crunchy movements like ELP and the Grandiosemovements like Yes, but still the band manages to maintain its own sound. It's got symphonic bits,ballad bits, even some neo-prog bits. Really something for everyone in the genre. The concept of The Whirlwind is all about the turbulence and struggles of life (like aWhirlwind).... but there's something in the eye of that Whirlwind to make it all good...And that something? It's Jesus. Unfortunately. Neal Morse has a bit of a track record for insertinghis beliefs into his music (as all artists do), but Neal does it in a very cheesy way. At the end of60 minutes of pretty solid prog rock (but not the strongest lyrics) we're greeted with a cheesyChristian Pop Rock 12 minute movement that's musically quite weak compared to the rest of the songand lyrically fairly cringe worthy. The Album overall has some religious motifs and undertones - and in general this is common in music- there's many biblical references across the Prog Rock Genre in some of the greatest works of alltime (Like Genesis' Suppers Ready), but Neal Morse unfortunately approaches this topic with zerotact - and to me, it spoils the entire album. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't the end of the song, all the build up and all that work just toend on what feels like a pushy, overly preachy pop-rock song about Neal's faith. If the final movement was in the middle of the song it'd seem out of place but wouldn't be tooegregious, but ending off the entire song undermines the whole Epic.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — To my (iperfect) knowledge, Saecula Saeculorum is one of the earliest Brazilian prog bands with OsMutantes, but this one is overtly symphonic. Their sole album appeared in the second half of the70's, but only completed or released in the mid-90's; and was rather short (30') by internationalstandards, but a fairly professional-sounding affair. One can think of a few classicUS/UK groupslike Yes, but the sextet featured the violin in the forefront, which can make you think more ofKansas or Richardson-era Caravan. However, the vocals are sung in Portuguese, which distinguishesthem semi-immediately (large parts of their music is instrumental); The album starts a bit with a liturgical ambiance before going grandiose & verbose with the albumlongest (8-mins) eponymous track, alternating between all-out rock and symphonic passages. The restof the album follows suit, though as newer tracks flow out of your Hi-Fi, less excitement from thesonwriting pours out. Viana's violin overpowers a lot of the music, except for the bass player, andthe odd piano romantic interludes. If you enjoy Kansas' music, this is in the same vein, but with anaxxentuated violin. Very interesting and happy to have known about this band in the last 30 years,but I wouldn't consider Saecula Saeculorum anything essential listening. So 3.5 stars really!!!

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — Actually, I am torn with regards to rating this album. For the top rating, the five stars, says "Essential: a masterpiece of progressive music". Ritchie Blackmore's Rainbow is not a masterpiece of progressive music, for it is not an example of "progressive music", really. It is a stellar example of "Elizabethan hard rock music", which is certainly a thing to consider, but taking that as "prog" would take my general tendencies of prog-folk-pastoral-renaissance-whatever crossover way too far. And yet. Prior to listening to this album, decades ago, I had no expectations. Rainbow was the band Blackmore started after leaving Purple, and I was thinking it's going to be your typical vanity project, a lot of guitar, way less sense. And boy, was I surprised. I can't really understate this - even compared to other hard rock albums I had heard by the time I first put on this record (I was probably fourteen, but I had been listening to rock for three solid years of active, voracious listening), Rainbow's debut stands out. EVERY song here makes sense. Every one is catchy, each and every one shows a different approach towards the hard rock paradigm. Even the two main ballads - Catch the Rainbow and Temple of the King - are completely different, the former being a melancholic, intimate tune whereas the latter is the nostalgic, solemn remembrance of things past. Also, I don't think Blackmore - the man behind Burn or Smoke on the Water - ever wrote anything better than the main stomping riff of Man on the Silver Moutain (and the arpeggios in the prechorus). Some say the approach would be perfected on Rising (I don't know, that one is a tad too uneven for me as an album), but even if that was the case, the blueprint is here - and like it or not, Dio has been more or less going to this exact well for the rest of his career.The album still sounds fresh after all these years. It stills sets the bar for "rock" for me, even in the aspect of general album consistency (where it dwarfs even Zeppelin, for example). Not a masterpiece of progressive music, but a masterpiece of rock music, deserving every star it gets.

Just one lengthy tracks lasting 40 minutes(this was before Thick As A Brick) and subdivided in 5 movements. The 40-mins composition (well at times, it's more like a blies-based jam) allows for plenty ofinstrumental freedom (but it's not instrumental music, be aware) and explore many differentclimates, but they don't go extreme-Eastern Asia ambiances (hence a misleading good-lookingartword), despite some modal passages. The vocals, however, are uneven, goind from good to crine-inducing.To say the least, despite throwing the word flower in their name, FTB was devinitely neither floralor subtle, but then again, it's all about power and psyched-out fumes. BTW, for years, I wascalling this album "Sartori", I guess, in memory of the Beat poets and Crimson's Beat release. Iwill round up to the fourth star, because it is that good , if you're in that kind of substance-fueled trip.

items.body: Review by ralphabet — October were a progressive rock band from Michigan who produced two privately-pressed albums c. 1979, both of which have become quite sought-after (especially since neither have seen an official reissue of any kind).I find this album a bit tricky to outright recommend, as there are some considerable flaws present. First of all, the production is extremely amateurish and frankly kind of bad. Everything is quite murky and a lot of the instruments lack much of an impact, which is particularly evident on the rhythm section. It's also let down by some weak singing (the intro to "Nero" being particularly egregious and borderline incomprehensible) on the few tracks with vocals.That being said, there's enough interesting ideas that I've relistened to this album multiple times, and I'm always surprised by how much I like it. I think the October albums are too obscure to have any kind of real "consensus" as to which of the two is better, but between this and After The Fall, this is by far my favourite. There's a playful, kind of jazzy undercurrent to many of the songs that I really like, further accentuated by the violin playing (which is the highlight of many tracks here).I don't know; the more I listen to this, the more grows on me. From an objective perspective this isn't really that great or anything, but if you find underground prog and private prog releases interesting, it'll probably be enjoyable for you. You can find better albums out there, but you can also do a lot worse than this.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Famous for its artwork "gracing" Julian Cope's book cover on Japanese rock, Anywhere is certainlyone of the iconic release from the land of the rising sin, partly because one of the earliest "ROCK"releases from the archipelago. Whether Anywhere is 'progressive" is debatable, because the music onit is derivative (like Toyotas and Datsuns were at the time), but it certainly is raw (very, sometimes), heavy andpsychedelic - so it should fit our scope well enough.It's even less "prog" that outside the intro and outro, the album is all made up of covers, most ofthem from bands we like (Sabs, Crimson, Animals & Co.), so it's relatively difficult to judge onthe band's originality, because they sometimes stick by the original (Black Sabbath and SchizoidMan), and at times they differ quite a bit (House of the Rising Sun) or extending in a bluesy jam ona Muddy Waters. But if that all-cover choice is not speaking of their inspirations, they do show the extent of thevirtuosity of the members at their rspective instruments. Pleasant album, but nothing essential, andtheir next Satori effort will be infintely better - in big part because it contains 100% FTBmaterial.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Synergy" is the third full-length studio album by Norwegian metal act Extol. The album was releasedthrough Century Media Records in August 2003. It�s the successor to "Undeceived" from June 2000 andthere�s been one lineup change since the predecessor as bassist Tor Magne Glidje has been replacedby John Robert Mj�land. Extol formed in 1993 and released a couple of minor pre-album releases priorto releasing their 1998 debut full-length studio album "Burial". "Burial" was followed up by"Undeceived" in 2000 and the two albums feature the same quintet lineup and a relatively similarsounding technical/progressive death/black metal hybrid style.I�m sure it�s not only the bassist lineup change which has affected Extol�s musical direction on"Synergy", but it�s almost like listening to a totally different band compared to the sound on thetwo preceding album releases...and then again not completely, because Extol have kept some of thedefining features of their music and of course their Christian themed lyrics. Stylistically I�dlabel "Synergy" technical/progressive metal with elements from both thrash metal and death metal.The black metal influences found on the first couple of releases aren�t there anymore. The mostvalid and obvious musical influence is late era Death (the band) but the Australians in Alarum arealso a reference and Believer should probably be mentioned as an influence too.One of the few points of critique I had when reviewing the first two Extol albums was that theirsongwriting sometimes wasn�t concise enough and that their music lacked immediate hooks and althoughI don�t presume Extol have listened to me, it�s one of the things they have changed on "Synergy".Although Extol have generally increased the technical playing, the songs are shorter and more heavyand powerful. It�s a good example of an album where the technical playing hasn�t increased theinaccessibility of the music. Instead "Synergy" is both a technically well played, well produced,and very well written release which is both powerful and heavy, but also atmospheric and melodic.The shifts between raw shouting vocals and melodic clean singing also works well and "Synergy" isupon conclusion a high quality release from Extol and definitely a step up in quality since theirearly releases. A 3.5 - 4 star (75%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if the evocative title Twin Peaks infused the music with a sense of the uncanny through its reference to the Lynchian universe, the opening of "Where Do You Want Ghosts to Reside" calls to mind Pink Floyd; yet David Lynch's filmography is vast, and the atmosphere of Lost Highway also permeates the second track, "Surge." There, a commanding guitar riff asserts itself alongside a backing Mellotron, gradually building a martial mood reminiscent of Rush. The Polish quartet has plenty of aces up its sleeve, including a guitar melody from Michal Chalota that feels like something out of Rachmaninoff, dark and masterfully extended by the synthesizer. A Jethro Tull-esque hard rock section follows, featuring constantly shifting drum rhythms; by the time "Gorąca Linia" begins, the bass takes the lead, eventually yielding the spotlight to the piano. Oskar Cenkier shines here, playing with subtlety and holding his own against the persistent progressive hard rock guitar, from which a luminous melody eventually emerges."Pleonasm" soon reveals its deeply jazz-infused essence; Fren momentarily transforms into a trio where bass, drums, and piano become one, at times whispering, at others raising their voices. The moments when the melody slows down only serve to enhance the composition and its varied nuances; it is a pleasure to witness such diversity and the effective use of silence.When the guitar joins in, it does so within that same jazz framework; the rehearsed melodic lines are echoed by the piano before the group moves beyond improvisation to tackle a complex, progressive structure. The soul of "Pleonasm", and that of Fren itself, resides in both these phases. There are contrapuntal exchanges, first by the guitar, then the piano, later the drums, and finally the entire ensemble. The composition is clearly well-crafted, a fact that becomes increasingly apparent with repeated listening as the logic behind each section and its progression reveals itself. Another guitar riff of Balkan origin takes over, and its violence and fire are quelled by droplets of w�ter, which are, in fact, piano notes."Heavy Matter" weaves a symphony where the Mellotron and synthesizer vie to elevate the track, eventually giving way to a guitar-and-piano duet; together, they craft overlapping figures that build a complex melody, another fine composition that knows exactly when to pause and when to resume. "Time to Take Stones Away" recaptures some of that epic, yet unpretentious, Pink Floyd atmosphere found earlier on the album, aided by the guitar... though, as happens throughout the record, the piano disrupts those plans, to the listener's benefit, by introducing classical scalar runs reminiscent of the finale of Rick Wakeman's The Myths and Legends of King Arthur. Yet, the track never loses that symphonic-rock vibe, even as the melodies break free from convention to turn experimental during the trio sections. There are also echoes of the almost folk-like melodies found in the work of Keith Jarrett, Jack DeJohnette, and Gary Peacock, elements woven into the very fabric of the band's symphonic sound.

items.body: All I know is that when I’m with you all the lines they seem to blur I meant it when I said we were through But my heart isn’t so sure MODISTE could have built Nothing More Than a Machine inside a laptop, but the Louisville trio instead surrounds itself with analogue synthesizers, drum machines, and digital instruments from the 80s and 90s – machines with temperaments, imperfect memories, and knobs that invite somebody to reach out and make a decision. “Using these old machines is a small personal rebellion against convenience culture and all the small ways technology is sterilizing the creative process. Also, they’re just more fun. They’re unpredictable and wobbly and alive and have a certain warmth and texture that you just can’t replicate,” vocalist Sydney Sleadd says. Those influences are easy enough to hear. Depeche Mode, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Book of Love, New Order, Metric, The Motels, Tennis, Weyes Blood, and Strange Boutique all provide useful coordinates at different moments, although MODISTE’s strongest songs are the ones where those references begin to blur together. Sleadd’s voice supplies a recognizable center, Stein approaches synthesizers with the curiosity of someone who enjoys their peculiarities, and Stallings introduces enough guitar to keep the electronic arrangements physically grounded. That sense of play gives the album much of its character. Nightmare opens as though the closing credits of a 1987 prime-time drama have suddenly become an invitation, with broad synthesizer chords, bright melodic flourishes, and the faint suggestion that something romantic and vaguely dangerous is waiting around the next corner. As an instrumental, it establishes the album’s affection for period equipment without turning the record into an exercise in museum preservation. There is too much movement in the arrangement, and too much pleasure in the tones themselves, for that. Breaking My Own Heart brings Sleadd forward with a song about the exhausting arithmetic of wanting somebody who disappears whenever intimacy becomes possible. The verses maintain a cool exterior while the chorus gives her considerably more room, allowing the vocal to stretch across the arrangement as frustration turns into self-preservation. Beneath her, the electronics maintain an elegant tension between pop immediacy and emotional unease. The song understands how desire can survive well beyond the point at which common sense has packed its bags. On Blur, Dennis Stein’s synthesizers rise and recede while Kyle Stallings sends guitar through the open spaces, leaving Sleadd room to sing with poise, attraction, and wary self-knowledge. “We wanted Blur to have this ebb and flow that tapped into the feeling of not being able to pull away even when something isn’t good for you,” says Sleadd. The arrangement follows that idea closely. Synth lines swell and withdraw, the guitar adds an occasional flash of abrasion, and Sleadd sounds increasingly aware that recognition offers very little protection against repetition. The chorus catches the contradiction beautifully, with certainty dissolving beneath attraction. My Love heads into power-ballad territory with complete confidence. Sleadd leans into the emotional scale of the song, while the arrangement allows the chords to widen around her rather than crowding every available space. Its euphoric bridge provides one of the album’s most openly romantic moments, the kind of passage designed for a singer to look toward the back of the room and hold the note a little longer than expected. The instrumental Nightmare Part 2 then clears the air. Its spacious electronic architecture brings Jean-Michel Jarre to mind, particularly in the way melody and atmosphere are allowed to develop patiently across repeating figures. Where the opening Nightmare feels connected to television themes and eighties synth-pop drama, its sequel reaches toward something more expansive and cinematic, giving the album a useful midpoint before the songs return to their various romantic complications. Shadows finds MODISTE at its most theatrical. “Shadows delves into themes of longing, forbidden love, repressed desire, and surrender,” says Sleadd. “We wanted it to feel like a slow descent, similar to giving into temptation, with the synths and rhythm building a kind of hypnotic gravity around the words.” The song carries that descent in its pacing. Sleadd sings as though every warning has already been received, considered, and quietly placed to one side. Desire becomes a question of reputation, restraint, and the private thrill of crossing a line while knowing precisely where it was drawn. Shame gets powdered, perfumed, and sent onto the dance floor with a couple of spritzes of Tabu. Beneath the drama, the band keeps a firm hand on the arrangement, allowing the tension to accumulate without burying the lyric beneath excess. Age of the Andy brings one of the record’s strongest rhythmic turns, with a backbeat that carries some of Depeche Mode’s physical economy while Sleadd delivers one of her most assured performances. The keyboards have a harder edge here, and Stallings’ guitar adds pressure around the beat rather than competing with it. The result suits MODISTE particularly well: stylish, muscular synth-pop with enough space for the vocal personality to remain at the center. Besotted returns to the scale of a power ballad, though its emotional engine is a struggle over desire and control. Sleadd understands that these songs become more interesting when love comes with leverage, pride, hesitation, and the possibility of somebody losing the upper hand. The larger arrangement gives those tensions room to breathe, making the track feel less like a declaration than an extended negotiation between two people who know exactly how much power attraction can surrender. “In creating this record, we really discovered how well we worked together and how much we enjoy working together. We’re each pulling from different influences but there’s an overarching shared vision that is the glue of this project,” Stallings says. Listen to Nothing More Than a Machine below, and order the album here. Nothing More Than A Machine by MODISTE Their ambitions extend to the stage. “We’re really trying to create a full experience at our live show that allows everyone, including us, a reprieve from the day to day grind. While it’s a lot of work to pack out these big TVs, lights, and all of our stage production, it’s worth it to build an immersive world for people to come live in for a night,” Stein says. Nothing More Than a Machine earns its title through an affectionate contradiction. MODISTE loves machines because they can misbehave, drift, surprise, and require touch. Across the album, those machines become partners in songs about people behaving much the same way: losing control, guarding themselves badly, making familiar mistakes, and occasionally finding something beautiful in the trouble. Follow MODISTE: Website Instagram Spotify YouTube The post Louisville Synthpop Trio Modiste’s “Nothing More Than a Machine” Finds the Human Heart Inside Vintage Synths appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: We spend our lives never touching the trauma that we face, I never been proud but I take pride in knowing we radiate our darkest days The comfort that night gave us, as droplets from the rain remind us what we gain There is something almost perverse about how good Nocturnal Prose sounds while contemplating a world that seems determined to grind everybody into administrative paste. Droplets From The Rain, the second single from the San Antonio band’s debut album Western Interests, takes guitars built for nervous pacing, a rhythm section with the precision of a factory press, and Yole Centeno’s exhausted baritone, then points the entire apparatus toward memory: friends, trains, rain, trauma, survival, and those nights when misery somehow became bearable because somebody else was there. Centeno formed Nocturnal Prose after leaving screamo outfit Amygdala, and you can hear the residue of that background beneath the post-punk architecture. The emotional stakes remain high, although the delivery has cooled into something more drained and watchful. His voice sits low in the mix with the weary authority of someone reading the morning headlines after already knowing they will be terrible. Around him, guitarist Nick turns anxiety into movement, stretching chords until they seem ready to split, while bassist Aaron and drummer Chuy lock together so tightly that separating their contributions becomes almost beside the point. You can hear traces of classic 80s post-punk’s vocabulary throughout Droplets From The Rain: the wiry tension, basslines carrying their own emotional burden, and guitars equally capable of abrasion and sudden beauty. There is some of Asylum Party’s wounded romanticism in its atmosphere, while Red Lorry Yellow Lorry and Blitz can be felt in the harder rhythmic edges. Lowlife and For Against hover around the song’s deeper tonal spaces, where the bass does as much emotional work as the voice. Nick’s guitar, meanwhile, reaches toward the expansive playing associated with Chameleons and The Church, continually changing the emotional temperature rather than settling into one repeated figure. Chords stretch outward, smaller phrases scratch nervously around the verses, and eventually the instrument seems to break free of the song’s accumulated anxiety. Droplets From The Rain has enough personality to avoid becoming an archaeological dig through somebody’s record collection. The lyrics detail memories of companionship as a survival mechanism, with passing trains and rainfall functioning as the incidental music of people trying to keep each other alive. There is tenderness, but nobody is selling recovery as a motivational poster. Trauma remains avoided, carried, inherited, and occasionally transformed into pride because getting through a terrible period with another person can become its own small victory; the song carries some of Blade Runner’s rain-streaked finality. Droplets From The Rain shows that despair can have a bassline, memory can have momentum, and friendship can become a form of resistance. The song keeps moving because standing still would mean getting swallowed. By the time the final guitar line recedes, the comfort promised in the title feels provisional, fragile, and necessary. For a band staring straight at modern misery, that measure of grace feels enormous. Nocturnal Prose write from an America saturated with institutional violence, economic exhaustion, ICE raids and detainments, mass distraction, and the daily horror transmitted from Gaza through the same devices used to order dinner. Their response is deeply personal without shrinking into private misery. Listen to Droplets From The Rain below and order the album here. items.body: UK black metal festival Fortress Festival has confirmed a new batch of artists for its dungeon synth stage, which expands to two full days in the theatre room at Scarborough Spa for the event’s fifth anniversary. Fortress Festival 2027 takes place on 29-30 May 2027 in Scarborough, North Yorkshire, UK. Organizers said around 150 tickets remained for the two-day event as of the August 4, 2026 announcement. Leading the new dungeon synth stage confirmations is the worldwide live debut of French dungeon synth artist Erang. Discussing the decision to perform live for the first time, Erang stated: “This music is all my life, and I give everything I have to it. For the longest time, it has been such a solitary thing to craft. 2027 will mark the 15th anniversary of my first album, TOME I, and for the first time, I’ve decided to create a live performance around the Land of the Five Seasons. Because the people who enjoy my music have been asking for this for so many years, and their support is the only thing that matters to me: the Kingdom is Ours!” Dungeon synth stage lineup for Fortress Festival 2027 The dungeon synth stage additions announced on August 4, 2026 are: Erang (France) – worldwide live debut Wraith Knight (US) – UK debut and exclusive performance Spectral Castle (France) – live debut Hole Dweller (US) Atlantean Sword – had to cancel its planned 2026 appearance Lord Bakartia (Spain) DragonKeep (France) These artists join Fortress Festival’s dungeon synth stage alongside the festival’s already-announced main and Ocean Room bills, which are led by Norwegian black metal act Emperor in an exclusive UK headline performance. About Fortress Festival Fortress Festival is a black metal festival held at Scarborough Spa in Scarborough, North Yorkshire, UK. Its first edition ran over three days starting June 2, 2023, and the festival has continued annually since, with its 2025 edition selling out. The 2027 edition, spanning 29-30 May 2027, marks the festival’s fifth anniversary and is organized in partnership with Reaper Agency UK. Fortress Festival’s dungeon synth stage has grown alongside the wider bill, and the 2027 edition expands the format to two consecutive days in the venue’s theatre room. Dungeon synth itself traces back to the early 1990s as an offshoot of black metal, built around synthesizer-led, atmospheric, fantasy-themed soundscapes; Erang, one of the fifth-anniversary stage’s new confirmations, has been part of that scene’s revival since releasing his debut album “TOME I” in 2012.

items.body: Here’s a news that only reached us now. Death By Love released “In Unity (Wieloryb Remix and Tribute)” on 14 July 2026, a two-track single on Distortion Productions built around remixes by the late Polish industrial artist Wieloryb (Paweł Kmiecik), who died in June 2026. The release reworks “In Unity”, a track from the duo’s 2026 debut album “444”, and all profits go to support Kmiecik’s family. In Unity (WIELORYB Remix and Tribute) by Death By Love Death By Love bring a gothic-industrial and darkwave sound that mixes trip-hop pacing with Middle Eastern melodic elements, heard across their debut album “444”. “In Unity” was originally written by Inga Habiba and Peter Guellard for that record. For this release Wieloryb reworked the track into two versions: “In Unity (Wieloryb Vs. Psychotribe Remix)”, edited by Peter Guellard under his Psychotribe alias, and “In Unity (Wieloryb Power Noise Remix)”. Inga Habiba’s vocals carry over from the original, Guellard handled mastering, and Grindhouse Alternative Art Studio created the cover art. Wieloryb also directed the video for the Psychotribe remix before his death, released via Distortion Productions. Peter Guellard explained why the duo dedicated the release to Wieloryb: “We dedicate this release to Wieloryb, Pawel Kmiecik, an extraordinary artist, producer, and video creator, whose vision left a lasting mark on the industrial scene. ‘In Unity’ was the final remix he completed before his sudden and unexpected passing. His post-apocalyptic industrial landscapes sent chills down our spines, while his relentless rhythms and crushing soundscapes raised our pulse and demanded movement. His work was raw, uncompromising, and unforgettable. Thank you for everything Pawel. Your legacy lives on through the art you left behind. All profits from this release will go directly to support Pawel’s family.” The video for “In Unity (Wieloryb Vs. Psychotribe Remix)” is on YouTube. Wieloryb, the artist behind ‘In Unity’ Wieloryb was the project of Paweł Kmiecik, formed in 1994 in Poland’s Trójmiasto area (Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) and among the country’s earliest EBM acts. Its debut cassette, “1”, earned a nomination for the Fryderyk award, Poland’s main music industry prize, and the project went on to blend electro-industrial, EBM and techno with noise, metallic rhythms and ambient textures across releases including “2”, “3” and, in 2025, “No Flag” on Requiem Records. Side-Line interviewed Kmiecik about “No Flag” in January 2026, months before his death. About Death By Love Death By Love is a Polish-U.S. dark electronic duo formed by Polish singer-songwriter Inga Habiba and Polish-born, U.S.-based producer and multi-instrumentalist Peter Guellard, whose past work includes the Polish goth band Blitzkrieg and the U.S. dark-electronic underground. The pair’s collaboration grew out of a remix Guellard made for Habiba’s electronic act NUN Electro, which led to further work on her solo project CallMe and, eventually, to Death By Love. The duo signed to Distortion Productions in January 2025 and released their debut single, “Strong Inside”, the same month, followed by a cover of Maanam’s “Krakowski Spleen” in March 2025. Their debut album, “444”, followed on Distortion Productions in February 2026: an 11-track record combining gothic, industrial and trip-hop elements with Middle Eastern melodic touches, exploring mysticism, identity and spiritual tension. Its tracks include “Sellenno”, “Cosmic Power”, “In Unity” and “Temros (Symphonic Mix)”, a reworked version of a track that first appeared on the compilation “Electronic Saviors Vol. 7: ReUnion”. “In Unity (WIELORYB Remix and Tribute)”, released on 14 July 2026, reworks the album’s “In Unity” into two Wieloryb remixes and doubles as a tribute to the Polish industrial artist.

items.body: Chicago electronic trio Pixel Grip has announced ‘Percepticide: Remixed’, a remix package built from their 2025 album “Percepticide: The Death of Reality.” The self-released project rolls out on Bandcamp, opened by Glasgow-based producer KAVARI’s rework of the album track “Noise,” released July 10, 2026, with the wider package following on July 29, 2026. Noise (KAVARI Remix) by Pixel Grip ‘Percepticide: Remixed’ tracklist and contributors “Percepticide: The Death of Reality,” released independently on June 12, 2025, was Pixel Grip’s third studio album and first fully self-released record, running twelve tracks: “Crows Feast,” “Bet You Do.,” “Stamina,” “Reason to Stay,” “Insignificant,” “Noise,” “Moment with God,” “Split,” “Last Laugh,” “Work or Shut Up,” “Jealousy is Lethal” and “Gonna Be Faster.” For “Percepticide: Remixed,” each of those tracks is reworked by a different producer, with some, including “Reason to Stay,” receiving multiple versions. Confirmed contributors include KAVARI, Perel, Curses, Auragraph, Frazer Ray, Matrixxman, Mercy Girl, Fire-Toolz, Black Asteroid, Inhalt, club.drippy, A Thousand Mad Things, Majick, Ole Mic Odd and Normal Bias, alongside a Pixel Grip self-remix. KAVARI’s version of “Noise” reworks the original into a harder club arrangement. Pixel Grip is Rita Lukea on vocals with Tyler Ommen and Jonathon Freund handling production, active since 2018. Earlier in 2026, the band contributed a remix of Nine Inch Nails’ “As Alive as You Need Me to Be” to the compilation “TRON Ares: Divergence”, released alongside contributions from Mark Pritchard, Boys Noize, Lanark Artefax, Chilly Gonzales and other artists. No CD or vinyl edition of “Percepticide: Remixed” has been announced; the release is confirmed for digital release via Bandcamp only. About Pixel Grip Pixel Grip formed in Chicago, Illinois, in 2018, built around vocalist Rita Lukea with producers Tyler Ommen and Jonathon Freund. The trio’s sound draws on electropop, darkwave, minimal synth, coldwave and EBM, shaped in part by Chicago’s queer club and disco scenes. The band released its debut album, “Heavy Handed,” in 2019, followed by “Arena” in 2021. “Percepticide: The Death of Reality” arrived on June 12, 2025, as Pixel Grip’s third studio album and its first release without a label, described by the band as a record built around betrayal, trauma, rage and reconstruction. In February 2026, Pixel Grip contributed a remix to “TRON Ares: Divergence,” the various-artists companion project featuring new material from Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross alongside Nine Inch Nails. With “Percepticide: Remixed,” Pixel Grip extends the “Percepticide” era into a second, fully collaborative release, handing the original album over to a wide field of electronic producers for reinterpretation.

items.body: Toronto aggrotech act Mission Divide released the single “Plaything” on Bandcamp on 7 August 2026. The digital release pairs the original track with a remix by Sean Beesley of Live Evil Productions, and closes out the project’s Flesh Collection series of singles. “Plaything” runs 3:58 and was written, produced and performed by Mission Divide. The release adds a second version, “Plaything (Live Evil Get Down Mix),” a 4:43 rework credited to Sean Beesley of Live Evil Productions, a Toronto-based production and remix outfit. Bandcamp tags the release as electronic, aggrotech, dark electro, hard techno and industrial techno. According to the release notes, “Plaything” concludes, for now, Mission Divide’s Flesh Collection series of singles. ‘Plaything’ remix by Live Evil Productions The Live Evil Get Down Mix marks Mission Divide’s latest collaboration with a Toronto-based remixer, keeping the project’s release pattern of pairing new singles with a single guest rework rather than issuing multi-remix EPs. No further formats or physical editions have been announced; “Plaything” is available as a digital streaming and download release on Bandcamp. Plaything by Mission Divide About Mission Divide Mission Divide is a Toronto, Ontario project combining aggrotech, techno and industrial elements. No founding date, member names or label affiliation have been published; releases have gone out independently through the project’s own Bandcamp page. The project’s Bandcamp discography traces back to “Happiness Is Fleeting,” released 14 April 2023, followed by “DANSE” and “Mechanical Lust” the same year, then “Wasteland” in September 2023. “Resolution” followed in February 2024, the “PHASES” release in August 2024, and “The Devil’s Got A Gun” in October 2024. “Look At Me” arrived in October 2025, followed by “Die For You” in July 2026. “Plaything,” released 7 August 2026, is Mission Divide’s most recent single and the project’s first release to receive Side-Line coverage.

items.body: Division:Dark, the anonymous industrial metal collective from Germany, released the single “The Curse”, the fourth track from their upcoming second album, “The Eternal Baptism”, out October 2, 2026 through Metalville. Division:Dark’s ‘The Curse’ single “The Curse” continues the sound of “The Eternal Baptism”, combining powerful guitars, modern industrial rhythms, orchestral elements and electronic sound design into what the band describes as an approach that is “as emotional as it is monumental.” The twelve-track album, previously led by the single “Caught In The Loop”, builds a concept around a dystopian society that has suppressed human emotion, with its title “baptism” symbolizing what the band calls a “return to the lost human frequency.” As with the rest of Division:Dark’s output, the musicians behind “The Curse” remain unnamed, with the project presenting itself as an anonymous collective rather than a fixed line-up. About Division:Dark Division:Dark is an anonymous industrial metal project from Germany that pairs heavy guitars, electronics and cinematic arrangements with an ongoing science-fiction narrative. The collective released its debut album “Prophecy” on February 11, 2022 through Drakkar Entertainment, a digipak CD built around a different guest vocalist on each track, including Blutengel’s Chris Pohl, Megaherz singer Lex, Otto Dix, Vicky Psarakis, Anna Murphy of Eluveitie and Anneke van Giersbergen. With “The Eternal Baptism”, Division:Dark move from Drakkar Entertainment to Metalville and shift to a self-contained concept album, with “The Curse” arriving as the second single after “Caught In The Loop” ahead of the record’s October 2, 2026 release.

items.body: Swedish electronic act Twice a Man will release “The Marine Trilogy”, a 48-page 2CD artbook compiling out-of-print, marine-themed material recorded between 1984 and 1986, on October 23, 2026 through Dependent, limited to 500 copies. Twice a Man’s ‘The Marine Trilogy’ artbook The tracks originally appeared on the cassette “Waterland” and the 12″ singles “Aqua Marine Drum” and “Across The Ocean,” releases that have since become sought-after collectors’ items. “The Marine Trilogy” gathers and remasters that material for its first appearance on CD. Pre-sale for the artbook begins September 9, 2026. The band describes “Waterland” as the result of a collaboration with the Center for Studies of Whales and Dolphins, which recorded the whale sounds used as the bassline on “Across the Ocean.” Twice a Man frame the material around the marine world as “a perspective from which to view the world,” made amid what the band calls its “fear of the turbulent world order” of the mid-1980s. The group also confirmed a new full-length album is in the works, to be announced separately. About Twice a Man Twice a Man is a Swedish electronic duo from Gothenburg, formed by Dan Söderqvist and Karl Gasleben (born Ingemar Ljungström), who met in the early 1970s playing in the groups Älgarnas Trädgård and Anna Själv Tredje. The pair started working together in 1978 as Cosmic Overdose, renamed the project Twice a Man in 1981 and released their debut album, “Music For Girls,” in 1982. From 1984 the group began incorporating samplers into its synthesizer-based, theatrical sound, a period that produced the marine-themed “Waterland” cassette and the “Aqua Marine Drum” and “Across The Ocean” singles now collected on “The Marine Trilogy.” Long-time collaborator Jocke Söderqvist rejoined the group in 2013. More recently, Twice a Man released the video for “Dahlia” in 2023, remastered former member Lars Falk’s classic 1980s-era material, and in 2025 announced the album “The Coloured Breeze Is a New Dimension,” led by the single “Birds Eye View.” “The Marine Trilogy,” due October 23, 2026, revisits the band’s mid-1980s marine-themed recordings ahead of a new full-length album still to be announced.

items.body: Tender Ender, the solo project of Swiss artist Thomas Schmidiger, released the single “Darkness”, accompanied by a self-directed music video, ahead of his second album, “Red Kites”, due November 13, 2026. The single is also available to stream via iMusician. Tender Ender’s ‘Darkness’ single and ‘Red Kites’ album “Darkness” is built around a home organ and its built-in rhythm section, a duet pairing Schmidiger’s baritone with the breathy vocals of Sabine Ruch. Schmidiger describes the track as “a living-room-sized hymn,” where the home organ “rolls out the carpet for a soothing daydream of escape,” and compares its mood to dark chocolate: “bittersweet, velvety and uplifting.” Schmidiger also directed the accompanying video, shot during the annual wheat harvest and the swarms of red kites that gather over the fields afterward. He explains the imagery came to him ready-made: “It was basically ready-made,” he says of the harvest and the birds, adding that the scene “somehow summed it all up.” “I like boring things,” he says. “They tend to open doors you didn’t even know existed.” “Darkness” is the first single from “Red Kites”, out November 13, 2026 and available to preorder on Tender Ender’s site. About Tender Ender Tender Ender is the solo project of Swiss artist Thomas Schmidiger, blending film-noir pop, ambient melancholy and piano balladry built around a home organ, enriched with harmonium, vibraphone, pedal steel and piano. Less than a year after his debut album, Schmidiger returns with “Red Kites”, due November 13, 2026, led by the single “Darkness” featuring vocalist Sabine Ruch.

items.body: Hungarian darkfolk act Cawatana released “Real, Open (NCN2026 Version)” on August 7, 2026, a reworked version of the track recorded as a teaser for the band’s upcoming performance at NCN Festival in Deutzen bei Leipzig, Germany, on September 6, 2026. The new version was recorded by Kiss Balázs in July 2026 and combines acoustic guitars, accordion, live percussion (both acoustic and electronic), drum machines, analog synths and bass guitar, aiming for an “organic” sound rather than a conventional electronic treatment. The release includes both the full “Real, Open (NCN2026 Version)” and a radio edit, and is available as a name-your-price digital download on Bandcamp and to stream on Spotify. About Cawatana Cawatana is a minimal synth and darkwave band from Hungary, blending post-punk, new wave and post-folk influences. The project originally started in 1999 and has performed in its current form, built around analog synths, drum machines and sequencers, since 2018. Its recent releases include the album “Beyond The Glory” in June 2025 and “We Live Silently (Major Analog Version)” in November 2025. “Real, Open (NCN2026 Version)” continues that run and points toward the band’s September 6, 2026 appearance at NCN Festival in Deutzen bei Leipzig.

items.body: Danish electropop act deZeption releases the single “Am I You” on August 7, 2026, through Town And Towers Records. The synth-driven track is built on shimmering synthesizers, driving beats and atmospheric production, and its lyrics are set in the near future, following a humanoid robot that begins to question its own existence as it reflects on the boundary between man and machine. Town And Towers describes “Am I You” as a single that “blends infectious electronic rhythms, lush soundscapes, and thought-provoking lyrics about identity, humanity, and artificial intelligence.” The release is the latest step in deZeption’s ongoing work as a solo project of Jan Brink, who is currently writing material for the band’s third album; “Am I You” is not confirmed as part of that album at this stage. deZeption pairs ‘Am I You’ with a ‘Human Eyes’ vinyl reissue Alongside the new single, deZeption’s 2008 debut album “Human Eyes” is reissued on 12″ vinyl, available through Elastic Stage. “Human Eyes” was originally self-released on CDr in 2008 on deZeption’s own deZeptivemusic label and was positively received in Denmark, Germany and Norway; Town And Towers reissued the ten-track album digitally in September 2024, and the new vinyl edition follows that reissue. Human Eyes by deZeption About deZeption deZeption was formed in Denmark in May 2003 as a part-time project by Jan Brink and Claus Lindeskov Hansen. The duo’s debut album, “Human Eyes”, followed in 2008 on their own deZeptivemusic label and was positively received in Denmark, Germany and Norway, leading to concerts in all three countries. Kim B. Sommer joined as a live keyboard player in May 2005 and was subsequently made a permanent member; he later left to form the band Synthnoter. Lead singer Claus Lindeskov Hansen left deZeption in August 2011 and later revived his music under the name enter.me. Henning Wibrand joined as deZeption’s new lead singer in July 2012. The band’s second album, “Mature”, followed in 2017, alongside a music video for the track “While the Wind Blows”; Kim B. Sommer left the band the same year and went on to join Synthnoter. This “new” deZeption line-up played its live debut in 2018, and Jan Brink and Henning Wibrand ended their collaboration in October 2019. Morten Kristensen of the Danish electropop act Disrupted Being has also played live with deZeption. Since 2019, deZeption has continued as the solo project of Jan Brink, who writes, produces and sings under the name, describing the band’s sound as “futurepop with an edge.” Brink signed deZeption to Town And Towers Records in 2024, which reissued “Human Eyes” digitally that September and released the new singles “No Sense” and “A New World Is Rising.” Side-Line has covered deZeption’s work under Town And Towers since the signing and “No Sense” release in June 2024 and the “A New World Is Rising” single in November 2024. “Am I You” continues that run and arrives as Brink works on deZeption’s third album, with the “Human Eyes” vinyl reissue marking the album’s first physical pressing since its original 2008 CDr release.

items.body: The Chameleons released their debut studio album, “Script of the Bridge,” through Statik Records on 8 August 1983. The English post-punk band from Middleton, Greater Manchester, recorded the album at Cargo Studios in Rochdale with engineer Colin Richardson. “Script of the Bridge” turns 43 this year. The classic Chameleons line-up of Mark Burgess (bass, vocals), Dave Fielding (guitar, keyboards), Reg Smithies (guitar, cover artwork) and John Lever (drums) is credited as producer alongside Richardson. Statik issued the album on vinyl LP and cassette, opening with “Don’t Fall,” which samples dialogue from the 1946 film Two Sisters from Boston, and running twelve tracks through to closer “View from a Hill.” The record includes the singles “Up the Down Escalator,” “As High as You Can Go” and “A Person Isn’t Safe Anywhere These Days.” In the United States, MCA Records issued a truncated eight-track edition under the name Chameleons U.K, omitting “Here Today,” “Less Than Human,” “Paper Tigers” and “View from a Hill.” “Script of the Bridge” streams on Spotify in its full twelve-track, remastered form. About The Chameleons The Chameleons formed in Middleton, Greater Manchester, in 1981 when bassist and vocalist Mark Burgess, guitarist Reg Smithies and guitarist Dave Fielding began playing together without a drummer; Smithies and Fielding had previously performed together as Years, while Burgess came from the Cliches. Middleton drummer Brian Schofield joined briefly before John Lever, formerly of the Politicians, took over on drums, with former Magazine drummer Martin Jackson filling in during 1982-83 while Lever was on sabbatical. After a 1981 session for BBC Radio 1 DJ John Peel, the band signed to Epic Records and released the Steve Lillywhite-produced debut single “In Shreds” in March 1982, its sleeve painted by Smithies, who created the artwork for all the band’s releases. Epic dropped the group soon after, and the Chameleons signed to Statik Records, a Virgin Records subsidiary, on which they released “Script of the Bridge” on 8 August 1983. Statik’s status as a Virgin subsidiary kept the album off the UK independent charts, but a truncated MCA Records edition built the band a college-radio following in the United States. The Chameleons followed with a second album, “What Does Anything Mean? Basically,” on Statik in 1985, then signed to Geffen Records for “Strange Times” in 1986. The death of manager Tony Fletcher in 1987 and internal tension between Burgess and Fielding led the band to split that year; Burgess and Lever went on to form the Sun and the Moon, while Smithies and Fielding formed the Reegs. The Chameleons reconvened in 2000 for shows at the Witchwood in Ashton-under-Lyne, released the acoustic album “Strip” the same year and the studio album “Why Call It Anything” in 2001, before splitting again in 2003. Burgess and Lever went on to perform the band’s catalogue as ChameleonsVox from 2009 until Lever’s death in 2017. Burgess and Smithies reformed the Chameleons under the band’s original name in 2021 with guitarist Chris Oliver and drummer Stephen Rice, both previously of ChameleonsVox, releasing the live album “Edge Sessions (Live from the Edge)” on Metropolis Records in 2022, the label the band joined that February. The reformed lineup, rounded out by keyboardist Danny Ashberry, announced a December 2022 UK tour and toured with Au Pairs singer Lesley Woods in 2023. In May 2024 the band released the “Where Are You?” EP, their first new material in over two decades, followed that October by the “Tomorrow Remember Yesterday” EP of re-recorded early tracks. The Chameleons released the single “Saviours Are A Dangerous Thing” via Metropolis Records in May 2025 ahead of their fifth studio album, “Arctic Moon,” released that September, and announced a European “Arctic Moon” tour for the fall. More than four decades after Statik released “Script of the Bridge,” the guitar-driven, atmospheric sound the album established remains the foundation the Chameleons’ later work continues to build on.

items.body: The Italian group Contrastate originally formed in the late 1980s. Over the years, and through line-up evolutions, this Experimental outfit has built up an impressive discography, with numerous releases appearing on a variety of labels. This latest work takes us back to 2014, when the band intended to compose a Soundtrack for a film that ultimately never came to fruition. The music, however, endured and was finally completed and released more than a decade later as a collection of eight tracks. Contrastate is known for its uncompromising Experimental sound, yet on this album it is clearly noticeable that the material was conceived as a film Soundtrack. The record is highly varied, shifting between minimalist electronic sequences and a genuine patchwork of sounds. At times, Contrastate creates an unsettling atmosphere, only to let it evolve into passages with a subtle Jazzy feel, supported by gentle rhythms. Field recordings are also present throughout the album, alongside occasional industrial elements. The album possesses a distinctly Cinematic quality, inviting the listener to imagine their own story and accompanying film. For me, this is accessible Experimental music that remains engaging without sacrificing its adventurous spirit. (Rating:7). Listen to “The Tongue Of Fire”: The Tongue Of Fire by Contrastate About Contrastate Contrastate is an experimental group formed in 1987 in London by Stephen Meixner and Jonathan Grieve, joined in 1992 by Stephen J. Pomeroy. The project grew out of earlier work under the names The Disciples of Delmonte and The State Organisation, drawing on the industrial and experimental music scene of the 1970s and 1980s as well as experimental film, theatre, and writing. Contrastate was inactive between 2000 and 2010. Releases have included “A Breeding Ground for Flies” and its 2016 vinyl/CD companion “No Eden Without Annihilation”, assembled from live recordings made across Europe between 2012 and 2014. The group’s latest album, “Seven Flies Feeding Inside The Tears Of A Woman’s Eye”, released on FinalMuzik, revisits music originally written in 2014 for an unrealized film soundtrack.

items.body: Tempus fugit . A number of up and coming adventurous saxophonists who once surprised with their original voices suddenly, it seems, have been around for quite a while now. Immanuel Wilkins, Stacy Dillard, and Caleb Wheeler Curtis, the subject of this review, by now have expansive discographies. Wheeler’s album The True Story of Bears and the Invention of the Battery was listed as a top album of 2024 on the Free Jazz Collective by one reviewer. Ritual , for goodness sakes, is the multi-instrumentalist’s sixth album as a leader . And it’s so easy to lose track and just call a musician “new.” A case study for mistaken novice is the pianist on this record, the legendary Orrin Evans. Evans had anchored the Philadelphia jazz scene and had been a mainstay in New York’s jazz community for decades when he won Downbeat’s Rising Star award. It was great for the maestro to get some long overdue recognition, but remains one of the most baffling episodes in the history of that magazine’s historic poll. Evans after all, by that point, was already serving in a mentor capacity to Caleb Wheeler Curtis, signing him to Imani Records. Ritual advances the narrative even more, as this is the first album as a leader Curtis has recorded for a label other than Imani, going this time with Chill Tone Records. Ritual is a beautifully free-roaming album that is somehow simultaneously tightly controlled. For me, there are two standout tracks on this album: the first, “Fantasmas,” and the last, the title track “Ritual.” “Fantasmas” is a wonderful rubato ballad for which Curtis composes a traditional AABA theme. Despite the thematic jacket, the piece just meanders and floats in a sea of rhythm and atmospherics. The rhythm is largely thanks to drummer Michael Sarin, who on this album often chooses not to simply play time. The atmospherics are mainly the result of a stunningly powerful guitar performance by Emmanuel Michael. Together, Sarin and Michael remind me of the ECM Paul Motion and Bill Frisell albums. Joe Lovano often was the horn player on those ECMs, while here Caleb Wheeler Curtis’s tone is much more hard edged, made a little sharp and prickly by his saxophone of choice: the stritch. Wheeler’s website cites possibly a more accurate reference point: Wheeler “draws from a wide range of influences including progressive bop and post-Coltrane/Ornette free improvisation.” Actually, one might say a song like “Fantasmas” is like Ornette Coleman playing with Liberty Ellman. “Ritual” is a stunning composition that leaves bold seams of silence intact throughout. After a mournful eight note melodic line, this time featuring Curtis on trumpet, multi-instrumentalist Henry Paz on flute, and Vincente Archer bowing the double bass, the band stops playing for a full four seconds–and this four seconds of silence contains so much weight and power as I listened for when, or if, the band would return. These gaps are slowly filled in by the musicians: first Curtis on saxophone, then Sarin on drums, and finally Emmanuel Michael’s guitar. The album, I should note, is more straight ahead than some followers of the FJC may want it to be. While there is tremendous freedom on the record, even those who loved The True Story of Bears may find Ritual to be quieter and tamer by comparison. And don’t mistake my point, I love the two tunes referenced above, but this album is filled with beautiful songs (check out “Florence,” “Pond,” and “The End of Power,” for instance). The Bandcamp page for Ritual says Caleb Wheeler Curtis “celebrates the ritual and practice of communal music making,” and this should appeal to those of us who love this music not so much for its virtuosity, but for the kind of world it imagines and makes possible. A ritual provides solace through routine. I would like to imagine our world in such dedicated practice of community that doing so becomes routine. Ritual can be ordered here: https://calebwheelercurtis.bandcamp.com/album/ritual Ritual by Caleb Wheeler Curtis Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
TUIDE are giving fans their first look at all seven members in action. The new girl group unveiled Meet my GRLS, TUIDE, their first performance video ahead of their official debut. The visual features 'GRLS', a track from their upcoming debut EP, TUNE & PLAY, which arrives on 24 August.

Made up of SEOHEE, SEOYEON, ELENA, JIA, SAKI, SEAH, and YI HANI, TUIDE are the first act from ABD, HYBE MUSIC GROUP’s new label specialising in girl group production.

Built around an energetic garage rhythm, 'GRLS' introduces the seven members one by one before bringing their individual personalities together through its recurring “Meet my girls / Me & my girls” hook. Its choreography draws from house, hip-hop, and soul, while the video moves between colourful interconnected spaces to spotlight each member.

According to the group, the song embodies what they call their “bestie-tude” — a confidence rooted in individuality and the friendship shared between the members, who hail from Korea, the U.S., the U.K., and Japan.

TUIDE take their name from the phrase “Tune the Tide,” reflecting the group’s ambition to transform the different “tides” they encounter into new forms of joy through music.

items.body: Much of Europe goes on vacation in August, so there’s no better time to release an album about “adventure, travel, and the journey of life.” The Leeds post-rock quintet Din of Celestial Birds hopes their album will be the soundtrack to many road trips, ocean voyages and international flights. The music is not only good for Takeoffs & Landings, but the time in-between. As festival season approaches, one of these trips may be to see the band in person. There’s not a second to waste as the band jumps right into it with three guitars, synth, bass and drums. The music is upbeat and punchy, adding a secret weapon: this is also post-rock that one can dance to, despite its metal overtones; a keen sense of rhythm calls fans out of the mosh pit and onto the main floor. One suspects that this aspect of the music is largely responsible for the band’s swiftly-growing reputation as a stellar live act. At 3:11, “Takeoffs & Landings” is also the rare post-rock track that qualifies as a radio single. While the music is largely aggressive, veering from post-rock to math rock to progressive rock, the moments of dynamic contrast stand out. One of these arrives early in “Marmoris” when the music calms down enough for one to hear the sounds of the shore. As the bank of guitars resurfaces and the drummer viciously attacks his drums, a sense of catharsis is palpable. The well-named “When Suddenly …” races out of the gate like the opener, then stops at 2:06; for a split-second, one thinks the track has ended, when suddenly it shifts gears to establish a base of solo piano upon which all the other instruments will build; a light choir lifts the track to the stratosphere. Two of the best tracks also contain the best post-rock titles. The first of these is “From This Summit We Can See The Heavens & Stars,” whose opening minutes are remarkably restrained, to the extent that one wonders if the track had been considered for the opening slot. The attack arrives at 2:32 in a melodic, metallic surge. This is followed by a mini-synth breakdown at 3:10, which leads to a drum roll and the summit of the title; then at 5:08, just as the track is ending, an even higher peak. Highlight “I Hope That Road Leads You Somewhere Beautiful, Somewhere You Belong” succeeds with subtlety rather than bombast; reflecting its title, the music seems slightly melancholic, a love letter to the listener. August is not only the month for vacations, but transitions, implying endings and goodbyes. This piece speaks directly to the heart, setting up the multi-toned farewell finale, “Second Star To The Right, and Straight On ‘Til Morning.” Soon the vacations will be over, the kids will be back at school, and the earth will tumble farther from the sun, but not yet; may we cherish these halcyon weeks of takeoffs and landings while we still have them. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Benga runs on interlocking guitars and a rhythm that does not let up, the sound that owned Kenyan pop for forty years. Winyo has spent twenty of those years playing it his own way, guitar in hand, singing in Luo and Swahili in a voice his countrymen named after a bird. He plays The Jago in Dalston on Sunday 9 August, a room of a couple of hundred, and most of the set is an album he has not released yet. The one piece of the record anyone can hear so far is “Mapenzi Sumu”, released in April. The title is Swahili for love is poison, and Winyo wrote it after a ten-year relationship ended. He recorded it at Ketebul Music in Nairobi, the studio behind his 2012 debut Benga Blues, with Fiston Lusambo of Afriquoi on bass, guitar and arrangement, then sent it to London for Abubilla’s Elliot Wenman to add keys, piano, synths and drums. Winyo has said he normally writes behind metaphor and this time did not, and there are lines he can barely sing without stopping. Born Shiphton Onyango on the shore of Lake Victoria, he took the Luo word for bird as his name, and twenty years of singing benga have taken him onto stages with the likes of Gilberto Gil and Vieux Farka Touré, Joss Stone and into the studio with the late Oliver Mtukudzi. The London end of that record is Abubilla Music, the label behind Winyo’s return and the promoter of this show. Abubilla and Ketebul have been working together for over a decade on Singing Wells, hauling recording gear into villages across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda to get down music that was disappearing, and Winyo has sung on those sessions, sitting in with village groups and building new songs out of what they played. The Kenyan connection reaches the venue as well. Kwame Otiende has run The Jago since 2018, and he grew up between Nairobi and western Kenya, the Luo country where benga started and where Winyo was born. Dalston has been dancing to benga in that room for years. On Sunday it comes from a man who has spent twenty years keeping it alive.   Winyo plays The Jago in Dalston on Sunday 9 August Tickets are available HERE   The post Event Preview: Winyo @ The Jago (London; Sunday, 9th August 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: A low cello refrain runs under “A Quiet Pulse” from the opening, looping and insistent, the work of Redi Hasa. The track is the second single from Sound Sketches: Music Composed for the Giorgio Armani Privé 2005–2025 Exhibition, the new album from L’Antidote, out on 18 September through Ponderosa Music Records. Hasa had the classical repertoire down by thirteen, learned in Tirana on a state-owned instrument, and he says he loves betraying that training. The 1997 civil war cut his conservatory studies short, and he reached Italy the year after on a scholarship to Lecce, carrying a cello taken from the Tirana Conservatory, the one his 2020 solo record The Stolen Cello is named for. He and his two bandmates, Iranian percussionist Bijan Chemirani and Lebanese pianist Rami Khalife, recorded “A Quiet Pulse” live off each other with nothing written down. You can hear the looseness in how the parts arrive. The cello figure keeps returning, slow and even, the piece breathing around it. Chemirani comes in on the zarb, hand and shaker work skating over the top, and Khalife’s piano arrives late, thick with reverb and echo, before a cry cuts clean through the calm. The cry runs back through both men’s histories. Chemirani learned the zarb from his father, the Persian master Djamchid Chemirani. Khalife, son of the Lebanese oud player Marcel Khalife, was born in Beirut during the civil war. L’Antidote wrote Sound Sketches for the Armani/Silos galleries in Milan, to fill the rooms as visitors move through twenty years of couture. It is their second record, though they place it at the start of everything, the point where the three of them first played as one band. The trio took their name from what Khalife says music does: an antidote to reality, something that soothes and shifts how you see things. They tour through the autumn: 22 October at Santeria Toscana 31 in Milan, 27 October at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris, 28 October at the Teatro Cantiere Florida in Florence for the HEARTbeat Festival, and 17 November at sPAZIO211 in Turin. Stream and listen to “A Quiet Pulse” HERE   The post Daily Discovery: L’Antidote – A Quiet Pulse appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

NOX is also a bit special, because they started out after most of these post-rockattempts had ended and is still around in the mid-20's.Like most of Post Rock projects, the music developped is calm, dark, moody, sombre, ambient,instrumental, and often is cinematic and Nile On waX (that's the official spelling) doesn't divergefrom the principle. items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 3.5 stars. It would be four if they had only released 10 albums instead of 100.Okay, I am not entirely sure that anyone even gives a sh.. about this band. Are they even a band? How come they have made over 100 albums? These are all facts, according to my oracle, Google God, are true.So here is a 1st review of their music, on PA.I am not sure why I picked upon this album. The band is hugely prolific, as Ashtray Navigations, do they not even care what others make of their music? Indeed, if I had as many albums to my name as this band, I would not really care what people thought of my music. But they have nonetheless released a huge number of albums, over 100, That may or may not make them the most prolific band in history. I do not know the answer to that question, and am too scared to Google it. Just in case, it goes well beyond a mere 100 albums (I suspect it does), and is something ridiculous like 1000 albums, I simply do not want to know, the whole idea sets my mind affright.So what? You bored readers are wondering, does their music sound like?Well. I have just played their 2026 album Quad (probably one of the many albums from 2026) a few times over, and it is not the disaster zone that I had expected. Whilst it is not the best album I have heard so far this year, it is equally a very long way from being the worst. How do you sum this band up upon one single album? Well! Quite simply, you don't, you can't. How can you? So down to the music. I was astonished to hear tunes, decent enough tunes, even if nothing amazing came my way from the album. I was surprised that the music could hold my incredibly short attention span for more than a few minutes. The whole album clocks in at a merciful 44 minutes. I use the word merciful, for the simple reason that I could be spending my time listening to far better music than this (or could I?). That is in no way to say that this is bad music, it is not. I can just think of a few bands that I would rather be listening to. Yes, just a few.It is not as if this is bad music, indeed it is way more inventive than you would expect from a band with over 100 albums to their name. It is mostly that my presumption is that no band can release over 100 albums and yet still maintain any kind of momentum. Well. Ashtray Navigations has proved my theory wrong. Whilst this is not the best album I have heard this year, it is equally a really long way from being the worst.It is inventive in its deliverance and sound, It is like that interesting uncle who holds a Ph.D. in philosophy, and has a head full of great philosophical stories, that hold you rapt in attention because if you miss a single beat, you have no hope of grasping the import of that great insight. This album is way more than great background music, it is actually worth listening to. But, up alongside some of this year's better albums, it falls a bit short. But, honestly, not by all that much. It really is a rather good slab. A more than worthwhile excursion into the wonderful world of Ashtray Navigations. A great name for a band.�It still blows my mind that a band can release this many albums, and the one that I pick to listen to, really is a rather good work. Maybe I just got lucky? Who Knows? Least of all me.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — How these Swedish musicians ended up in PA's Heavy Prog gnre is one of the greatest mysteries sincethe Big Bang, because their sole album goes in all direction from the JR/F base. How NevarlLajf managed to find the Eastern French label for the release and distribution of their album is alsosurprising, but it remains explicable. How Klusterfloristen found its awfully ugly sleeve artworkis most likely due to the planet aligning the wrong way, ensuring a direct ozone hole for bad taste,but it can be forgiven, given the young age of the quintet.OK, their instrumental music is definitely fusion of all types of influences from classical, jazz,rock sometimes dominated from a crunchy guitars dual attack, but IMHO, th's the organ (ok viasynths) that leads the soundscapes towards avant-prog territories, without crossing that boundary.Outside the closing 11-mins Kyskhastsdisco track, the rest of the tracks hover between 3 and 7minutes, but there are tons of things happening in them, though nothing is revolutionary orgroundbreaking, but these young lads certainly knew how to lay a timeless 70's sonic ambiances.Somtimes, one can think a jam is developping, but the whole thing remains a bit too complex to allowtotal improvisation freedom.Originally, I'd bought this album some 10 to 15 years ago, but never got around to laying mythoughts about, but it turns out the disc got stuck in my car deck for about a week, so it was theonly thing I could listen until I finally managed to pop it out. Hence this review. Nothingessential, but if you like it complex, instyrumental and with some sonic humour (they're not Zappa,though).

It is definitely Jazz, 'but not as we know it, Jim'.This is an enigmatic band to put it mildly.They sound way more like they are from South America, but who am I to judge. They have a pretty slick Jazz sound that works for even me. I don't hate jazz, I would just rather listen to something else. This is a slightly strange album, (I think) but knowing so little about jazz, puts my whole perspective out of kilter. I generally know when I am hearing good new music, but that doesn't really apply to jazz and me. Yes, the music is hopelessly catchy, so I can only base my opinions upon that premise. I can only reiterate that I am not a fan of jazz, and will never play this album again. Except that I have stuck it on my playlist, so when it's time comes I can throw it out, as just another jazz album that I don't care for.But these guys do most certainly have something good going on... and this from a non jazz fan.I reckon that this could well appeal to all those who love 'pop' jazz with a definite twist. This is good music, that is hugely underappreciated. But what do I know, a non jazz fan?If you like catchy jazz with a twist, this will be right up your street. It really is excellent.
