items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 981Tangerine Dream is a progressive electronic rock band that was founded in Berlin, Germany in 1967 by Edgar Froese. Initially the band was formed as The Ones in 1965. Tangerine Dream is one of the electronic pioneers with a very extensive and amazing career. The work of them comprises several and different phases all over the years. The initial phase also called The Pink Years is the phase that is of interest for this review. As its name indicates, this is a musical phase a bit influenced by Pink Floyd. The albums that belong to that phase are the first four studio albums of Tangerine Dream, "Electronic Meditation" from 1970, "Alpha Centauri" from 1971, "Zeit" from 1972 and "Atem" from 1973.So, their initial phase began with an avant-garde and herb-rocking debut work, perhaps misleadingly titled "Electronic Meditation", because it's more a krautrock than an electronic work. In reality, it was only on their second studio album "Alpha Centauri" that the synthesizers came into play. Until then they managed to play without electronic instruments. Besides, the line up on "Electronic Meditation" isn't what is considered the classic line up of Tangerine Dream. In reality, it was only on their third studio work "Zeit" that appeared what is now considered the best line up of the band, Edgar Froese, Christopher Franke and Peter Baumann, because on their second effort "Alpha Centauri", Bauman wasn't present yet. So, "Electronic Meditation" appears to be quite a polarizing album between fans, due to that. After this album, each member went his own way, and each went on to be a renowned krautrock artist in their own way."Electronic Meditation" strongly deviates from all the other albums of the huge Tangerine Dream's catalogue. As I mentioned above, it's very ironic that "Electronic Meditation" was the only Tangerine Dream's album released in the 70's where its title didn't fit at all. It's neither electronic music made by synthesizers or meditative. The album consists apparently of experimental noises without a clear direction and purpose, performed with classic rock instruments. Nothing less representative could have been released as the debut of an electronic progressive act. In reality, this is a real rock album made with rock instruments. It's actually krautrock, the musical style invented by the German musicians in the late 60's and in the early 70's. "Electronic Meditation" is quite similar to "A Saucerful Of Secrets" and "Ummagumma" by Pink Floyd. Still, I also noticed the kind of music that Schulze later on would record with Ash Ra Tempel after he had left Tangerine Dream. Sometimes I even hear some hints of Jimi Hendrix, but also from their compatriots of Amon D��l, another krautrock German band from those days, one the best and most famous too."Electronic Meditation" has five tracks. The album starts with "Geburt (Genesis)", which is a track dominated by Schnitzler's scratchy creaking cello, combined with wild drumming and furious flute sounds performed by their guest, Keyserling. After a while something like a rhythm develops, but as soon as this is the case, the piece is already over and it goes straight and abruptly into its second track. The fittingly titled "Reise Durch Ein Brennendes Gehirn (Journey Through A Burning Brain)" begins as a freeform piece, then the organ enters with mighty tones, and finally the piece develops into a garish guitar orgy. This track encapsulates the whole krautrock vibe and it's a perfect example of crunchy rock and roll. This is probably the highlight of "Electronic Meditation". The pounding drums and acid guitar continue for "Kalter Rauch (Cold Smoke)". It begins with quiet organ sounds, which are repeatedly interrupted by short outbursts of chaos. Then the cello scrapes again, and snappy drums come and go, and another relentless psychedelic guitar attack ensues. I think it was mostly Pink Floyd that gave the inspiration to this track with its lengthy guitar/organ freak-outs. "Asche Zu Asche (Ashes To Ashes)" feels almost conventional compared to the rest of the album with a consistent rhythm and a halfway recognizable melody. The piece grows more and more furious with more distorted guitar over lazy cymbal heavy backbeat and, then suddenly, fades out. It reminds me a bit of The Doors. The concluding "Auferstehung (Resurrection)" begins with an almost solemn organ melody, to which a narrator declares a true incomprehensible text that was recorded backwards. In the further course, the theme of the opening track is taken up.Conclusion: Tangerine Dream is the best and most important electronic progressive act of the 70's and of all time, and they would over the decade make some of my all-time favourite music. Tangerine Dream is, next to Kraftwerk, the most well-known electronic formation in Germany. And just like them, they began almost entirely non-electronically. The first Tangerine Dream's album is quite a refreshing and experimentally quirky affair, quite different from the works that both Schulze and Froese later released. The five tracks are certainly worth listening to. I think the music here is probably better digested for many people than some of the material on their earlier real electronic albums. Besides, "Electronic Meditation" is a nice way to discover how Tangerine Dream started their career. And, all in all, the music on this album is probably a pleasant and interesting surprise, especially for those who are huge fans of the krautrock style of music.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

As you can see by the bands' genre designation (RIO/Avant-prog) this will not appeal to everyone. But! And, it is a huge BUT. This band has some real (dare I say it) catchy lines going on because they can write 'tunes'. The music is really not that far out. I would almost (though not quite) go as far as to say that this is 'progressive symphonic prog' in the sense that it is a genuine progression. The kind of symphonic prog that we all love, only from a slightly oblique angle. As much as we all wish that Genesis, Yes and ELP, etc had all written more great albums. They didn't. So here it is, the new pure sound of unadulterated Symphonic Progressive Rock.Here is an album that fully caries that torch of brilliance forward, into wholly new realms.This album has it, it is not bowing down to any former realms of music, it is a new creation. The way forward, the sound of now, pointing rockets at the sky. This is the future. This is Symphonic Progressive Rock.

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Coming to this album, I expected something much closer to the band's later soft rock sound. Like many listeners, I first knew Ambrosia through songs such as "Biggest Part of Me," so discovering their self-titled debut was quite a surprise. Rather than polished adult contemporary, this record presents a fascinating blend of melodic soft rock and progressive rock, creating an identity that feels both sophisticated and accessible. It easily exceeded my expectations.One of the album's greatest strengths is the balance between memorable melodies and progressive arrangements. While the music rarely reaches the complexity of the major symphonic prog bands of the era, it incorporates shifting structures, rich keyboard textures, dynamic contrasts, and tasteful instrumental passages without sacrificing accessibility. The result is an album that can appeal both to progressive rock fans and to listeners who enjoy melodic rock from the 1970s.The opening track, "Nice, Nice, Very Nice," immediately establishes this identity. Its polished production, layered vocals, and elegant keyboard work remind me at times of the atmosphere later associated with The Alan Parsons Project, while still maintaining Ambrosia's own personality. It is an excellent introduction and one of the reasons the album makes such a strong first impression.My favorite tracks are "Time Waits for No One," "Holdin' on to Yesterday," and especially "Make Us All Aware." The latter stands out for its stronger progressive character, interesting rhythmic development, and satisfying structural variations. Another highlight is "Mama Frog," whose instrumental approach occasionally brings to mind the energy of Emerson, Lake & Palmer and even some of King Crimson's more adventurous moments. The closing epic, "Drink of Water," is another outstanding composition, giving me the feeling of hearing Crosby, Stills & Nash interpreted through a progressive rock lens. It is a beautiful and memorable conclusion to the album.Instrumentally, the album is consistently enjoyable. The keyboards and synthesizers play a central role, adding color and atmosphere throughout the record, while the vocals remain expressive without becoming overdramatic. The musicianship is polished, serving the songs rather than existing simply to demonstrate technical ability.Although the album incorporates obvious soft rock influences, I still consider it a genuinely progressive rock release. The frequent changes in mood, carefully crafted arrangements, extended compositions, and willingness to experiment separate it from conventional soft rock albums of the period. At the same time, it avoids excessive complexity, jazz-oriented improvisation, or the grand symphonic approach that characterized many of its contemporaries. That accessibility is one of its greatest strengths rather than a weakness.Lyrically, I did not focus closely on the individual songs, but they complement the reflective and uplifting atmosphere created by the music. Combined with the warm production and melodic songwriting, the album maintains a consistently pleasant listening experience from beginning to end.Perhaps the greatest compliment I can give this album is that I never find myself wanting to skip a track. There are no weak moments here, and each song contributes something meaningful to the overall flow. The atmosphere is inviting, melodic, and subtly adventurous, making it an album I continue returning to years after first discovering it.I would recommend this record to anyone who enjoys the intersection of progressive rock and 1970s soft rock. Listeners who demand highly technical, symphonic, or heavy progressive music may find it too restrained, but those looking for sophisticated songwriting with progressive touches should find plenty to appreciate.

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Nearly sixty years into their existence, legendary rock band Yes may never recapture that dynamic, extravagant and inspired edge that made them one of the defining prog-rock bands of the Seventies, but that doesn't mean there's nothing left of worth with the current line-up and their recent releases. Mostly driven by longtime guitarist Steve Howe, here aided by frequent contributors - keyboardist Geoff Downes, bass player Billy Sherwood, former Glass Hammer frontman Jon Davison and more recent drummer Jan Schellen - this incarnation of the symphonic institution (having navigated the loss of founding bassist Chris Squire and longtime drummer Alan White) returns with their fourth album together, and twenty-sixth studio work overall, 2026's `Aurora', that shows them still offering colourful, adventurous and melodic rock that many die-hard fans will enjoy.Title track `Aurora' is a glorious and slick opener, where fancy orchestration, calling to mind their 2001 Album `Magnification', swoons around Steve Howe's reaching guitar strains, Billy Sherwood honouring the tradition of the late Chris Squire's upfront bass rumbles and a flighty Jon Davison vocal. Joyful with rousing reprises of striking themes, it makes for a memorable and impressive opener about evoking transformation and connection, and damned if "Like paper doves in a cut-out world..." ain't a darn adorable lyric!Despite lovely group harmonies and little pockets of fancy instrumental touches, `Turnaround Situation' doesn't hold together particularly well as a whole, but there's lovely buoyant bass and fancy acoustic flourishes racing alongside each-other throughout the dreamy and romantic (and better) `Love Lies Dreaming', perhaps vocally and musically one of the prettiest pieces of the disc.Being the longest track on the album at near fourteen minutes will instantly pique the interest of most prog-rock fans, but...lower that eyebrow, mister! Sadly the four-part `Countermovement', contemplating human authenticity, comes across as more a collection of fragments and half-completed passages rather than a coherent and flowing whole, but there are a nice range of tempo-shifts back and forth, and a lot of focus put on both Steve Howe's humble and pensive vocal and a range of versatile guitar solo spots.With `Ariadne', Yes adopts a storytelling approach of so many prog bands old and new, looking to myth and legend for inspiration, and it suitably surges forwards with Jan's strident drumming and delicate orchestration that soars with classical fancy. At its heart it recounts the mythological Greek tale of Princess Ariadne and the Minotaur's labyrinth, which the band also uses it as a metaphor for being lost, with lines like "With walls around you, you're trapped in your own space", and finally taking control. Howe's guitar adds a heroic flavour and urgency, and it's nice to hear group harmonies from several members together throughout.Despite a fairly banal lyric about springing to action, `All Hands on Deck' is quite fun with jaunty keyboard/guitar interplay, made memorable by Steve's guitar grunt that takes on a bluesier toughness in little bursts, and it's nice to hear Jon singing a little more naturally deeper throughout too! In what could probably be considered an interlude, the three minute `Outside the Box' is primarily an instrumental. Framed by a constantly morphing set of wordless sighing group harmonies, they're interspersed with an eclectic grab-bag of fuzzy electronic swirls, jamming bass/guitar duels and intricate drum patterns across a range of tempos back and forth.Short and sweet, soft-rocker `Emotional Intelligence' opens with gentle piano, unassuming acoustic strums and the warm hum of Hammond organ, Davison softly offering a call to understanding and unity with its well-meaning lyric. It briefly springs up to life near its climax with slide guitar wisps, and this compact little album closer displays restraint and tastefulness throughout.All versions of `Aurora' come with two pieces that are classed as bonus tracks, but they are actually both worthwhile inclusions that don't disrupt the flow of the core album or come across as mere throwaways. `Jambustin' (really just a fun way to refer to being `cut off'), is a warning against negative behaviours and arguing with or obstructing others, displaying a jauntiness in its verses and a softly grooving chorus with slinking bass. Despite a fairly overused motive of moving water as a metaphor for life and the passing of time, `Watching the River Roll' embraces the theme with acceptance and peace, and it delivers dreamy and shimmering instrumentation (not to mention constantly drifting Moog solos!) and bristles with an upbeat, life-affirming positivity that glides with energy.Yes has always had more to offer than just the contributions of former vocalist Jon Anderson and keyboardist Rick Wakeman, and modern, worthwhile work from both of those artists can easily be found elsewhere, so their absence doesn't take anything away from this current version of the group. Some pockets of the fanbase will find their exclusion absolutely inexcusable, meaning there's no coming back from that, but Yes has constantly had an eclectic revolving door of imaginative, skilled and varied musicians that have all made exciting contributions to the overall Yes sound throughout the decades.Despite being a little overlong and delivering a couple of less successful pieces, Yes have delivered an enjoyable disc of vibrant and eclectic rock in `Aurora', always melodic without falling into overtly poppy or radio-friendly banality and full of interesting instrumental details. Given several re-spins, it proves to be valid addition to the Yes legacy, with the current incarnation looking to their past but still moving forward in interesting and rewarding ways, and if you appreciate the wider world of Yes music from a range of musicians, chances are you'll find much to enjoy here.Three and a half stars.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Undeceived" is the second full-length studio album by Norwegian metal act Extol. The album wasreleased through Endtime Productions in June 2000. It�s the successor to "Burial" from December 1998although the two full-length album releases are bridged by the November 1999 "Mesmerized" EP. Therehas been no lineup changes since "Burial", so it�s the same quintet lineup who recorded "Burial",who also recorded "Undeceived".Stylistically Extol have developed upon the hard-to-define extreme metal style of their debut albumand Undeceived is another interesting hybrid death/black/progressive metal release from the band.The Christian themed lyrics are still in place but Extol for the most part keep their lyrics incheck and make sure they are not preachy/praise God type Christian themed lyrics. These lyrics dealmore with mental struggles, temptations, and how to overcome various issues in your life (by findingthe light/Jesus/God). The first thing you notice when listening to "Undeceived" is how well playing Extol are. These guysperform their music with great skill and conviction and both the harsh and the clean vocals whichare present in the music are also well performed. The sound production values are also on a highlevel, providing the material with the best possible platform to shine. The songwriting is variedand challenging but maybe lacks a bit in the immediate catchiness department. The more you listenthe more you remember the songs, but it�s not an album featuring big hooks. Upon conclusion Extol are arguably an intriguing band and "Undeceived" is a good quality releasefrom them, but their songwriting could prosper from a more concise formula. We always praise band�sfor being progressive and incorporating a lot of sections and different time signatures, but to myears Extol is a band who are best when they play their most simple and atmospheric parts. That�swhen their music has most impact. A 3.5 star (70%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4.5 stars. I have a strange relationship with this band (then again, that is true of every band that I listen to). I generally put all my albums (some 2,500 or so, many more sit in the sidelines waiting for me to pick them up again, post removal from my playlist) on random play, so I frequently forget who the band is that I am playing. It ends up being a game of Russian roulette (no pun intended). Like hearing an album for the 1st time, except that you know the music, but can't remember the artist. I must confess to being blown away sometimes by a Roz Vitalis album that comes up randomly, and at other times thinking what the heck is this Rubbish. This is all of course down to how receptive my head is at that moment in time. All good music has its place in my playlist, but my head is not always up for some of the completely wild atonal stuff that is on my playlist. Whilst Roz Vitalis are certainly not in that category, of being for very specific moments, they have enough of an edge to sometimes make me love them and other times not want to play them. Whilst this may sound bad for my love of this band, that is quite simply not the case. Sometimes I love the Beatles, or some early Bob, but not all the time.So what do I make of this 25th anniversary record? Well, as it uses some of the highlight tracks from their vast opus, there are tracks on here that I do already know, but some of the arrangements have me guessing. I would say the band have played it fairly safe for long-term fans, it is a great idea to mix some old material with new sounds. I would also say, for sure, that this is a great introduction to a band that can push its sonic boundaries well beyond anything that they have done here. This is not to denigrate this record, I just feel that they wished to capture the more listenable side of their music, as opposed to alienating everybody with a full on expose of just how weird and wonderful their sound can be at times.Violinist, Vitaly Borodin certainly deserves mention, I only know his work with Vespero (another great Russian band), but will happily seek out the other bands he has played in (they being The Legendary Flower Punk & Vevil). He, as the rest of the band do, appear to have all had an obvious classically trained background. Still, the man sticks some really great solo work into this recording, that bares no real resemblance to what I think of as Classically trained violinist as doing. He plays an almost gypsy style (which I love) that overrides his classical training.So to sum this album up!Well, I would say that it is definitely a great gateway into their music, for those who have perhaps been put off in the past by their more oblique albums, (personally I love the more out there stuff. But! Only if I am in the mood). It is also great to hear some old tunes rearranged, especially with Vitaly Borodin on board, the band have really let him do his thing, as only he can do.This is definitely an album worth listening to if you have the slightest interest in music that pushes boundaries, but does not smash them to pieces, at least not here. (Totally free on Bandcamp as of writing this). This is a great place to start for such a diverse and original band. Not too much weirdness, but just enough for those sat on the fence to go for it. The recording quality makes it sound, at least, to my ears, as if it was recorded in a studio. Others may have a very different take on that thought, it is just my opinion.A great 25th anniversary recording.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Within by Protest The Hero is the band's most progressive and melodic album to date, but still keeping their mathcore, punk and post hardcore energy. Musically the band are still shredding at tempos that would make cars jealous, with some great impressive melodic and harmonic guitar playing. Vocalist Rody Walker's voice has strengthened with each release, almost as if the band has a new vocalist, with his cleans being like a mix of Claudio Sanchez & Rob Halford. Their songwriting has improved too, with even more progressive leanings, showcasing longer and more atmospheric compositions, without any loss of energy. Also it's a short, sweet and to the point album, with it only being over half an hour long. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is The Mariner.

Those albums felt a little too staleevery once in a while.But, luckily, SEI really did give me a sense of Maschera taking a leap in the right direction. Iimmediately noticed that the album had more varied orchestration than its predecessors. The bandutilized more instrumental textures and arrangement variation throughout the whole runtime of thisalbum, which makes it feel more lively. There are more parts that show movement in the keyboarddepartment, acoustic guitar driven sections come up more frequently, and in addition to the flute,other wind instruments joined the party. That's a huge step up imo, from the quite undercookedapproach that relied mostly on overdriven hammond organ, guitar and rhythm section with occasionalsynths. Super cool stuff!

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The Norwegian duo of H�kon Oftung and Kristian Fr�land continues to craft increasingly rich and subtle works. Following an introduction titled "Invokasjon", which could well serve as a compendium of the entire repertoire to follow, "Sankeren" kicks off with a sharp, aggressive electric guitar attack; yet, as H�kon Oftung begins to sing, those strange harmonies, so characteristic of Wigwam and practically patented by the Finnish band in the 70s, hovering somewhere between sacred music and atonal contemporary classical, start to emerge amidst the Minimoogs and Mellotrons. Then comes a section featuring a clavinet and a rhythm bordering on heavy metal, albeit in a symphonic vein, with arpeggios reminiscent of Mike Oldfield's Tubular Bells. The balance between instrumental and vocal passages is remarkable; after such high-speed intensity, an almost jazzy calm sets in, intimate and steeped in nocturnal darkness. Having steadily evolved their compositional style since 2017's Jord, by the time Salighet arrived, Jordsj� had truly come into their own."Salighet I", with its blend of acoustic guitar, flute, and clavinet, possesses the modern feel characteristic of the later Gryphon era; yet the album's defining feature is the work of the two musicians, a duo with such deep familiarity and seamless sonic and instrumental interplay that they take the Wigwam formula a step further. They are worthy successors, as their acoustic guitar and flute excursions brush against acoustic psychedelia before shifting abruptly into a new section, such is the richness of the album's musical vision. Bass clarinets and oboes also make themselves heard, creating an unusual atmosphere that reminded me of Marty Ehrlich's 1999 album Sojourn.In "Salighet II," on the other hand, the electric guitar and keyboard seem to tell a story; there is something mystical, an aura of discovery, as well as suspense, yet whether the music is in a slow or fast section, the momentum never flags, nor does the listener's attention. The flute enters at just the right moment, as does the clavinet.By the time the fifth track, "Ura," arrives, the mood is fully set; the polished precision reminiscent of Tubular Bells blends with the mysterious guitar notes in the vein of Jukka Tolonen. Towards the end, the guitar strums in isolation against a swelling keyboard, the air grows heavy and dense, while the Minimoog improvises, hovering between progressive rock and jazz-rock. Medieval darkness gives way to a frenetic, syncopated rhythm that stumbles and rises, stumbles and rises, gradually finding its own groove. In "Danseritualer fra Jordsj� - Prosesjon & Ekstase," the pastoral flute appears like a rainbow, only to be obscured by a free-form psychedelic interplay of bass and electric guitar."Stjernestigen" takes a dramatic turn, evoking a classical-leaning Chick Corea, yet there is something truly special about that oboe, the acoustic guitar, which later shifts to electric, and the impeccable vocals. The music unfolds with a Minimoog reminiscent at times of Wakeman and a jazzy piano flowing like a fresh breeze, all wrapped in an eternal mystery, one they will not reveal, for perhaps it is better that way; having learned the lesson of the past, they understand that the continuation of an unfinished ending holds the greatest promise of eternity.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — References to Emerson, Lake & Palmer are unavoidable in "The Seven Movements of the Third Majesty", the first of three tracks making up the second album by Ring Van M�bius (themselves a trio). Yet, starting with "The 3rd Majesty," they truly make the 70s sound their own, playing with such feeling, emotion, and conviction that they earn the right to wear their influences openly. After all, there is a fine line between merely copying a sound for convenience and channeling an influence born of years of listening and a genuine love for the genre, a path to finding one's own voice that even the greatest bands have walked, and one that ultimately comes down to the individual listener's taste. The surging Minimoog lines, the frenetic, air-slicing drums, and the bass advancing like a blitzkrieg leave no doubt; shifting from rock-style Hammond organ to jazzier tones, the only thing left to do is enjoy the superb musicianship and the fresh melodies, melodies that resemble constellations in the cosmos. Just as the scientific community discovers new ones, isn't that the perfect terrain for progressive rock? Space constellations... suddenly, the tempo slows, leaving the bass, drums, and Thor Erik Helgesen's vocals floating as if in a sci-fi series.Around the midpoint of the track, the organ takes on a distorted sound, accompanied by bass and drums that turn psychedelic, and at times they abandon their polished approach for a raw sound, losing the melody and improvising; the same applies to the vocalist, who lets loose and screams, not like Hammill, but in his own style, lending the music a vibrant, original character.Things get heavy towards the end of "The Seven Movements of the Third Majesty"; the organ takes on an atonal, distorted sound, reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator, marking the moment Ring Van M�bius truly comes into its own as a trio. It is not just about their playing, but also their composition and passionate execution, the third pillar of a great band on a great album."Illuminati" may continue to evoke Tarkus in their instrumental work, but Thor Erik Helgesen's vocal style leans closer to Deep Purple, yielding a completely different result; then they shift into jazz-rock, and a Renaissance-style section takes over, followed by instrumental passages featuring electric clavichord underpinned by drums and bass, the likes of which one might think we would no longer hear these days. Yet, the raw Norwegian intensity of the performance makes it feel new, original, and fresh. When the vocals need to be high-pitched and delicate, they deliver just that, and in the span of a mere five minutes, "Illuminati" manages to encompass the feel of multiple different songs."Distant Sphere" features a string section, and the shift in texture works beautifully; the arrangement is highly original, as is the way the trio enters immediately after, creating a space-like atmosphere with bass and Rhodes keyboard. When the drums kick in, it sounds like a trio featuring Bill Bruford, John Wetton, and Dave Stewart. The composition here is far more experimental, it is hard to believe it is just a trio, with the keyboard once again distorted to the point of frenzy; meanwhile, when they play jazz, they do so with an admirable groove, proving themselves worthy heirs to the Norwegian tradition in this regard as well. They also infuse the music with an ethereal, mysterious quality characteristic of space rock, a genre that influenced 1970s jazz-rock, and now influences them."The M�bius Ring" is a Yes-style rock track featuring Chris Squire-esque bass work; yet, when Thor Erik Helgesen sings, he makes the song his own, imbuing it with the band's signature stamp, a noble wildness reminiscent of fur coats and boots. The keyboards provide a grand, symphonic finale that gives way to the bass, where H�vard Rasmussen proves himself every bit as virtuosic as his bandmates. On drums, Dag Olav Hus�s even plays the timpani to mirror Thor Erik Helgesen's vocal inflections. It is a majestic journey, driven by a Minimoog line that stretches toward the horizon, where the sky meets a sea teeming with monsters promising unforgettable adventures, before looping back in a circular path: like a M�bius strip, like a ring, and like the trio's discography, which was just beginning here.

items.body: Feel it now and don’t resistThis time the anger’s better than the kissI must admit when so inclinedI tend to lose it than confront my mind Some songs that become so closely associated with their original performers that covering them feels a little like borrowing somebody else’s leather jacket. You might fit into it, you might even look terrific, but everybody remembers who wore it first. The Afghan Whigs’ Debonair is one of those numbers, loaded with Greg Dulli’s particular combination of seduction, self-disgust, and barely concealed bad intentions. Seattle’s Ghosts in the Graveyard approach it with enough confidence to make the jacket theirs. There is also something pleasantly strange about hearing an Afghan Whigs song pulled toward deathrock. The original already had danger baked into its bones, so the transformation feels less like genre tourism than discovering that two people from different neighborhoods have been drinking at the same questionable bar for years. The band gives Debonair a harder goth-rock frame, pushing the guitars forward while electronic accents gather around the edges. Byron C. Miller sings with the dramatic authority the material requires, leaning into the song’s appetite for trouble without treating Dulli’s original performance as sacred text. Paul Morgan’s guitar work supplies much of the momentum, moving between muscular chords and sharper details while the arrangement maintains the nightclub immediacy that has become central to Ghosts in the Graveyard. That relationship becomes clearer in the accompanying video, directed and edited by Miller and shot by cinematographer Ryan Purcell. The band performs inside a small club surrounded by an enthusiastic audience, with the camera catching bodies pressed toward the stage and musicians feeding off the room. Rather than turning the performance into an elaborate visual concept, the clip concentrates on physical proximity and the chemistry between band and crowd. It gives Debonair the slightly dangerous communal charge that rock music tends to acquire when there are fewer than six feet between the singer and somebody holding a beer. Watch the video for Debonair below: The cover will close Ghosts in the Graveyard’s forthcoming Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected, due this October through Re:Mission Entertainment. The record revisits the band’s 2016 album for its tenth anniversary, rebuilding the material from the ground up following the expanded reach of 2025’s Absolute Death. With Miller joined by Morgan, keyboardist Kaylie Cortez, and vocalist Shelly Smith, the current lineup has developed into a formidable live unit, something the Debonair video makes immediately apparent. Choosing this song as the album’s final word makes sense. Debonair has always sounded like somebody smiling while making several decisions they will regret tomorrow morning. Ghosts in the Graveyard preserve the song’s wicked little grin, then surround it with bigger guitars, gothic drama, and the welcome possibility that someone in the front row may lose a shoe. Listen to Debonair below and order the single here. items.body: Somewhere along the line, coldwave became frighteningly good at keeping its shirt tucked in. The drum machines behave, the bass sits precisely where expected, everyone owns an appropriate black coat, and occasionally you begin wondering whether an entire subculture has been sentenced to spend eternity posing beside the same concrete wall. Then along comes Mercury Girl with Low Altitude, sounding sufficiently nervous to remind you that this music once existed because somebody had something eating at them. Mercury Girl is the project of Filipino American San Diego musician Aaron Pena, whose debut album, A NuTone, arrives October 10. Low Altitude is its first single, and anxiety is practically another instrument in the arrangement. The drum machine keeps clipping forward at odd little angles while synth lines twitch overhead, creating the sensation of machinery functioning perfectly while its operator quietly considers pulling the emergency brake. Then there is that bassline, lofty and strangely buoyant beneath Pena’s dissonant vocal, which seems emotionally several rooms removed from the comparatively hopeful chords surrounding it. A guitar eventually climbs through the arrangement with considerably more grandeur, briefly opening the ceiling before everything settles again into the song’s peculiar state of suspended agitation. Black Marble, Harsh Symmetry, Molchat Doma, and Oppenheimer Analysis provide obvious relational coordinates, yet Pena understands the essential reason those records work: electronics can be emotionally merciless precisely because machines have no obligation to console anybody. Put a vulnerable voice beside a rigid drum pattern and suddenly every beat sounds like another second you have survived. “This song reflects on a breakthrough I had when coming to terms with my depression,” says Pena. “I wanted to write a song capturing the internal isolation I’ve felt within me for a long time while echoing the catharsis I had after fully acknowledging it.” Which could have produced a painfully earnest five-minute therapy session set to synthesizers, an occupational hazard of anybody writing openly about their own head. Pena has enough musical sense to leave the feelings inside the machinery, where they become stranger and more useful. Low Altitude carries its emotional trouble through repetition, distance, and those unexpectedly optimistic chords, suggesting the peculiar moment when understanding yourself provides relief without magically solving anything. Listen to Low Altitude below and order the single here. Low Altitude by Mercury Girl Recorded at home in San Diego, A NuTone will expand upon Pena’s experiences with depression, isolation, love, and the difficult business of accepting affection when your own brain occasionally argues against the proposition. Low Altitude makes an excellent introduction because beneath all those cold machines sits an old rock-and-roll problem with a very human soul, trying to figure out how to live inside himself. items.body: Chasing patterns Warnings and the like Recognizing signs You can see them too Some records are best understood by the room they create around you. Hermaphrodite, the new album from Phoenix industrial artist YZBL, turns that room into a place where the walls feel close, the floor seems unstable, and every beat lands with the private force of a thought you would rather keep buried. YZBL, pronounced “Jezebel,” has carried some of this physicality since her time in industrial goth trio Tassel, yet the music here feels newly concentrated, as though every spare element has been pulled toward one central question: who gets to decide what a body means? The album’s third single, “Patterns,” brings dub and trip-hop deeper into YZBL’s industrial vocabulary. The beat moves with a narcotic drag, leaving enough empty space for the low end to feel enormous, while the heavier passages suggest Godflesh filtered through the nocturnal unease of Tricky. There is also a funereal beauty in the surrounding textures that brings This Mortal Coil to mind, especially in the way density and delicacy can occupy the same few seconds without smoothing each other out. Where others might find only pain in dysphoria, YZBL finds a kind of power. Androgyny and hermaphroditism are words the artist reclaims deliberately. Her interest is not in a body that is read by others, but about a life built apart from those readings entirely Across Hermaphrodite, dysphoria runs alongside a hard-won sense of power. YZBL treats androgyny and hermaphroditism as reclaimed language, terms used to clear space away from the gaze of people eager to classify the body. Her writing approaches identity with the bodily directness of Kathy Acker: intimate, confrontational, occasionally ugly by design, and alert to the violence hidden inside ordinary categories. The record’s minimal rhythms give those ideas room to breathe, while drones and thick guitar weight make the questions feel physical rather than academic. The album’s core ultimately challenges the binary, not only externally imposed but also internalized by the artist. “I am most transphobic towards myself,” they controversially say, describing a lifelong war fought against the idea that “difference” is wrong. That physical unease reaches its sharpest visual form in the black-and-white video for Patterns,” made by YZBL and Ash Barrett. The camera finds her in a dark, abandoned, dungeon-like space, lit by a single bulb as she scratches marks into the surface around her. The imagery carries the raw panic of The Blair Witch Project, but its performance-art severity belongs to YZBL’s own world: part confinement, part self-documentation, part evidence left behind. Watch the video for Patterns below: Hermaphrodite‘s force comes from the solidarity underneath all that weight. YZBL writes from a place where no assigned category, chosen identity, or outside reading can fully contain a person. By turning that uncertainty into rhythm, pressure, and language, she makes ambiguity feel less like a void than a territory worth defending. Existing on your own terms becomes a form of possession: of the body, of the room, and finally of the name you choose to answer to. Out now through Lana Del Rabies’ Feral Crone Recordings, the album makes its title part of the argument. The word is intentionally loaded, reclaimed, and held up as a declaration of life beyond somebody else’s categories. items.body: It comes back to control me What it said is stuck on me It comes from the shadows So elusive to me Portland duo Princess Ugly approach labour as something closer to possession on their new single, The Work, turning the ordinary language of obligation into a study of creation, anxiety, and control. J. Christopher-Rome’s lyrics begin with familiar pressures: unfinished tasks, the reluctance to ask for help, the nagging sense that something remains unresolved…before those pressures acquire a strange agency of their own. Work ceases to feel like an activity and begins behaving like a presence, capable of following its creator home. Christopher Moncrieffe builds that unease into the arrangement through clipped electronic rhythms, stern bass movement, and the mechanical forward motion of classic EBM. There is enough post-punk space around the instrumentation for Rome’s voice to carry the psychological weight, while the programming maintains a physical momentum suited equally to headphones and a crowded club. The tension comes from how naturally those two impulses coexist: the body is encouraged to move while the mind gets trapped inside a recurring thought. Rome delivers the words with the exhausted concentration of someone attempting to identify a fear while still living inside it. Memory becomes another form of labour, something requiring constant maintenance before it can be trusted, and even dreams appear subordinate to productivity. Images of dust, unfinished construction, and something sharp waiting in the dark give the song an almost metaphysical dimension. Creation rises out of debris, yet the resulting object seems capable of turning upon its maker. The song recognizes a contemporary condition in which occupation, identity, output, and self-worth have become increasingly difficult to separate. You build something, maintain it, remember why you started, and eventually discover that the structure has developed requirements of its own. Princess Ugly allows that cycle to remain unresolved, which suits a piece concerned with repetition and the unease of never reaching completion. Watch the video for The Work below: Listen to the Leæther Strip Remix of The Work below and order the single here. The Work (Leæther Strip Remix) by Princess Ugly Claus Larsen pushes those instincts toward the dance floor on the accompanying LEÆTHER STRIP Remix. His version thickens the percussion and sharpens the electro-industrial attack, giving the track a harder, more immediate propulsion without losing its underlying dread. Larsen treats the original’s anxiety as fuel, transforming psychological pressure into movement. Together, the two versions make The Work feel less like a conventional song about employment than an examination of creation becoming obligation, obligation becoming authority, and authority eventually learning how to follow you home. items.body: “Cold fear making you feel inside” is an odd line to dance to, which is precisely why it suits Scary Nights, the new single from Dream Council, the Berlin-based project of Sean Michael Pheanis. The song belongs to that useful strain of synth-pop in which pleasure and unease share the same room, each sharpening the other. Its hook is immediate, its beat clipped and insistent, and its synths carry the lacquered cool of an 80s television performance viewed at midnight with the volume turned higher than wisdom recommends. Pheanis has been moving toward this music for years. Raised in the Chicago suburbs, he began in DIY punk, putting out friends’ recordings through a homemade label before a MicroKORG and the records of Adult., The Faint, and Fischerspooner redirected his attention. Bachelor Party Weekend followed, mixing dance-punk with an eccentric new-wave bounce, after which New York and the early Bushwick witch-house scene supplied another vocabulary. Later came Los Angeles, where the city’s darkwave community helped Dream Council settle into a clearer identity, and then Berlin, where Pheanis completed the project’s self-titled debut LP. That history can be heard in Scary Nights, though the song carries its references lightly. There is something of The Human League, LCD Soundsystem, and even a little Thompson Twins in its vocals and catchy melodics, while the sterner club architecture recalls modern contemporaries Buzz Kull, Kontravoid, and Blone Noble. Synth-pop works best when the machinery serves a memorable tune. The chorus has the tidy inevitability of a phrase one seems to know before hearing it, and the arrangement keeps finding small ways to increase the pressure around it. This song is catchy as hell. The accompanying video extends that sense of private unease. Pheanis appears alone in a club after closing time, moving in slow motion through a space built for crowds, flirtation, and communal release. With nobody left to watch, the dance becomes stranger and more personal. Empty floors and dormant lights turn the nightclub into a temporary kingdom for one, a place where fear can be indulged, stylized, and perhaps exhausted before morning. The conceit also gives the song a sly visual joke: dance music has finally secured the dance floor it always wanted, only to discover that absolute freedom can look suspiciously close to isolation. Watch the video for Scary Nights below: There is an appealing continuity between the song and Pheanis’s long sequence of relocations. Chicago, New York, Los Angeles, and Berlin each contributed something to Dream Council, and “Scary Nights” gathers those years into a remarkably assured piece of pop writing. Mixed by California engineer Frank Royal and due on the forthcoming self-titled album through Lollipop Records, it suggests an artist who has finally found the right room for all the music he has been carrying around. Listen to Scary Nights below and order the single here. items.body: So many things to learn, so many to unlearn To be in company and to be alone So many things I thought I cannot live without Now are disappearing, now are dissolving like clouds Boris Kaplunovich has spent much of his life moving between places that might reasonably be called home. Born in Belarus, raised in Israel, and now based in Berlin, the musician from Totenwald and Day Clinic approaches his new solo project with the accumulated perspective of someone accustomed to departures, reinvention, and the strange persistence of attachment. Tall Grass, his latest single, turns those experiences toward something intimate: the possibility that certain people find one another despite geography, history, and timing conspiring against them. Released July 25th as the first single from an EP expected this autumn, Tall Grass began with Kaplunovich lying in an unruly patch of grass in the middle of a city park. The setting provides central tension: a pocket of accidental wilderness surrounded by streets, buildings, appointments, and all the machinery by which urban life keeps time. Kaplunovich considers love from a similar position, contemplating encounters that seem improbable until, in retrospect, they acquire the peculiar logic of inevitability. The lyrics move between learning and unlearning, solitude and companionship, loss and recurrence. Possessions and old certainties dissolve, while affection survives through smaller gestures: sharing rain, lying together in tall grass, accepting mistakes that may return. At its center sits the consoling thought that two lives might repeatedly find each other, regardless of when history happened to place them on the earth. An acoustic guitar establishes the song’s modest frame before the arrangement gradually opens around it. Electronic tones enter with care, and the post-punk influence comes through in the use of space, repetition, and an occasional chill in the instrumentation. Kaplunovich sings with the plainspoken intimacy of a musician who understands how much weight understatement can carry. His phrasing leaves room around individual words, giving the performance the feeling of thoughts still taking shape as they are spoken. Gratitude runs through Tall Grass, complicated by an awareness that permanence is largely wishful thinking. People meet, circumstances change, cities absorb their inhabitants, and affection becomes inseparable from the knowledge that every shared moment belongs to a finite sequence. Kaplunovich finds tenderness within that recognition without turning it into easy consolation. Robert Hanna’s black-and-white video places Kaplunovich among neglected corners of the city: empty lots, worn concrete, industrial remnants, and abandoned spaces whose original purposes have become difficult to determine. He carries his guitar through these locations as a solitary troubadour, while Hanna finds striking geometry in broken walls, open ground, and severe urban surfaces. The photography gives Kaplunovich’s isolation a cinematic scale while preserving the song’s close, personal character. Watch the video for Tall Grass below: Following last October’s debut single, Be Them All, and years spent sharing stages with artists including Micah P. Hinson and Matt Elliott, Tall Grass brings Kaplunovich’s solo direction into sharper focus. His subject is belonging, understood here as a temporary alignment of people, place, and time. For a few minutes, lying together in the grass is enough. Listen to Tall Grass below and order the single here. items.body: Spike Hellis Successor Over-Pop Spike Hellis’ self-titled 2022 debut LP was wild, unpredictable and unexpected. Part of what made the Los Angeles duo’s take on gnarly mutant body music feel so nervy and dangerous was its aggressive switch-ups, slamming from funky EBM into anxious synthscapes and moody sample cut-ups, all anchored by Lainey Chang and Cortland Gibson’s rancorous vocals. Paired with their furious live shows, which featured the duo crawling over a jungle gym of equipment while a neon sign invited you to dial 1-888-FKN-WEAK, it made Spike Hellis impossible to ignore. Chang and Gibson’s new LP Successor takes all the spite, all the sweat, and all the smart programming and arrangement that made them so compelling, and boils it down to an even more potent and addictive formulation. It manages the trick of being both very minimal and absolutely enormous; at any given moment there could be little more than a bassline, a sample and a smattering percussion sounds going on, but each of those disparate elements is tuned and positioned for maximum impact. Debut single “By God” places a funky cowbell and crushed synth stabs on top of its burbling synth bass for one of the most addictive grooves of the year, and that’s before the shouted and sung vocals lob the song into brand new territory. Simultaneously, the Art-of-Noise-through-a-mirror-darkly “Entirely Mine” folds its repeated vocal samples into new shapes, ardent and punchy, but also steady and focused. The sheer power of the record lies in its meticulous arrangement, how everything is placed in the mix, and the space left between each drum hit, shout, sample, or synth note. “Your Successor” doesn’t sound complicated, but there’s a wealth of variation in how Chang’s half-rapped vocals bounce off the off-kilter drum programming, the stereo spread of the slow moving background textures and the tiny ripples of digital artifacting that flow into the outro. It’s none of it accidental, whether at their most noisy (“Pareplaneta”, which explodes and then lets you sit uncomfortably in the echoes) or their most accessible (the surprisingly touching “Pillow Talk”, whose bright chirps and barks manage to sound melancholic) every element is purposeful, and adds to the strength of the whole. And that’s all before we get into how ferocious and ornery Chang and Gibson are on the mic. And what’s more, that ire is cutting, and as refined and strategic as any other aspect of the album. There’s a genuine meanness to the sing-songy chorus of “Temptation” (“Feels like every time we turn around/these two petty fuckers run their mouths”) that suggests that whoever Hellis are addressing knows they’re being called out and would do well to duck them going forward. It’s a sort of calm antipathy that can be righteous (“Enemy Lines”), menacing (“Unwound (Get Right)”), or disdainful (“No Bite”), but is never obnoxious, no matter how spicy or bitter it might come across. Successor is Spike Hellis distilled; all the raw energy, all the movement, all the combativeness of their debut is here, but made sleeker, and delivered in more calculated fashion. And bizarrely, it ends up being both bracingly intense, and a whole lot of fun to listen to. It shouldn’t be possible to sound this unbothered and cool and this savage at the same time, but here we are; Spike Hellis are working hard, but you’ll never see them sweat. Highly recommended. Buy it. Successor by Spike Hellis The post Spike Hellis, “Successor” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Here’s one we missed. French electro-rock duo Marigold has made its debut album, “Noir Boulevard”, available on all major streaming platforms since 20 May 2026. The band mixes new wave, electronic tension and rock energy, describing its own sound as sitting between Depeche Mode and M83. Marigold blends new wave and rock energy on ‘Noir Boulevard’ The duo describes its music as “a powerful and immersive sonic universe, blending new wave, electronic tension, and rock energy,” built on live experience the duo traces back to the early 2000s. “Noir Boulevard” is the pair’s first full-length release and marks Side-Line’s first coverage of the project. About Marigold Marigold is a French electro-rock duo whose sound draws on new wave, electronic and rock elements, with the band itself citing Depeche Mode and M83 as reference points. The project maintains an official YouTube channel, “Marigold ϟ,” which lists Montpellier, France as its base and describes the act’s style with the tags electro, rock, synthwave, coldwave, darkwave and new wave. The duo has extensive live experience dating back to the early 2000s. Its debut album, “Noir Boulevard,” became available on all major streaming platforms on 20 May 2026.

items.body: Futurepop act Assemblage 23 has announced a five-date European headline tour for October 2026, with Mari Kattman joining as special guest on every date. Tom Shear will bring material from the album “Null” to club venues in Germany and Sweden. Null by Assemblage 23 The tour follows summer festival appearances for Assemblage 23, including a performance at Amphi Festival. “Null,” the project’s tenth studio album, was released via Metropolis Records on 7 November 2025. Mari Kattman, joining all headline dates as special guest, is known for her solo work as well as her role in Helix, her ongoing collaboration with Tom Shear, and mastering work for numerous artists across the industrial, EBM and synthpop scenes. Tour dates for Assemblage 23 Assemblage 23 plays the following dates in October 2026, with Mari Kattman as special guest throughout: 20 October – Karlsruhe, Germany – Die Stadtmitte 21 October – Oberhausen, Germany – Kulttempel 22 October – Hamburg, Germany – Indra Musikclub 23 October – Jonkoping, Sweden – SektorF 24 October – Hannover, Germany – SubKultur About Assemblage 23 Assemblage 23 is the American electro-industrial and futurepop project of Tom Shear, who debuted with the album “Contempt” in 1999. “Failure” followed in 2001 and found traction in dance clubs, before Shear signed to Metropolis Records and released “Defiance” in 2002 and “Storm” in 2003. The 2007 album “Meta” produced the single “Binary,” which reached the Top 25 of the Billboard U.S. singles chart, and was followed by “Compass” in 2009, “Bruise” in 2012, “Endure” in 2016 and “Mourn” in 2020. In 2018, Shear launched Helix, a side project with vocalist Mari Kattman that blends electronics, organic instrumentation and vocal harmonies across trip-hop, dub, dream pop and synthpop influences. Kattman, based in Providence, Rhode Island, has also lent vocals to acts including Mesh, Psy’Aviah, iVardensphere, Aesthetische, Neuroticfish and Solitary Experiments, and released her own material through COP International and Metropolis Records. Assemblage 23 released its tenth studio album, “Null,” via Metropolis Records on 7 November 2025, preceded by the singles “Tolerate” and “Believe.” The October 2026 European tour, with Kattman as support on every date, brings “Null” to club audiences in Germany and Sweden following the band’s summer festival run.

items.body: Belgian electro-industrial act Suicide Commando releases “Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version)” via Out Of Line Music on 7 August 2026. The track is a collaboration with dark techno and EBM project DSTRTD SGNL, who rework the industrial architecture Johan Van Roy built for the original. Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version) by Suicide Commando “Destroyer of Worlds” first appeared on Suicide Commando’s most recent studio album, “Goddestruktor,” released in 2022, which reached number 9 on the official German album charts. For the SGNLS Version, DSTRTD SGNL apply their dark techno and EBM production approach to the track, reshaping its structure for club and festival play while keeping Van Roy’s original vocal and industrial framework intact. DSTRTD SGNL is the German duo of Stephan Kessler and Torben Schmidt, active since 2021 in techno, EBM and dark electro, with a catalog of singles, EPs and remixes released mainly through Infacted Recordings, including collaborative work with acts such as Ruined Conflict and Mängelexemplar. The release arrives as Suicide Commando marks 40 years of activity, having formed in 1986. The project’s recent anniversary release, “Collective Suicide Vol. 1+2,” gathers material spanning early demo tapes through reworked classics alongside the new track “Control & Consent.” It is available on limited colored vinyl and as a strictly limited Wooden Fan Box Set restricted to 200 copies, containing a Digipak CD, colored double vinyl editions of both volumes and a 36-page photo book covering the band’s history. Suicide Commando live dates Suicide Commando has confirmed the following live dates: 22.08.2026 – Sao Paulo, Brazil 29.08.2026 – Mexico City, Mexico 11.12.2026 – Bielefeld, Germany 12.12.2026 – Oberhausen, Germany 15.01.2027 – Barcelona, Spain 16.01.2027 – Madrid, Spain About Suicide Commando Suicide Commando is the solo project of Belgian musician and producer Johan Van Roy, who began experimenting with electronic music in 1986. He self-released demo tapes through the late 1980s before being signed by the German label Off Beat, where his 1994 debut full-length, “Critical Stage,” marked a turning point for the project. A second album, “Stored Images,” followed in 1995 and included one of Van Roy’s most enduring songs, “See You in Hell.” Van Roy co-founded the Dependent label in 1999, releasing “Mindstrip” in 2000, which reached number one on the German alternative chart, alongside the singles “Hellraiser” and “Comatose Delusion.” The 2003 album “Axis of Evil” was voted album of the year by the Deutsche Alternative Charts, and 2006’s “Bind, Torture, Kill” reached the top of the same chart on the strength of the single “Godsend + Menschenfresser.” In 2009, Van Roy signed Suicide Commando to Out of Line Music, releasing the 7″ “Severed Head / Until We Die” followed by the EP “Die Motherfucker Die,” which also topped the German alternative chart. “Implements of Hell” followed in 2010, then “When Evil Speaks” in 2013, “Forest of the Impaled” in 2017 and “Goddestruktor” in 2022, which reached number 9 on the official German album charts. For live performances, Van Roy is joined by Torben Schmidt on keyboards and Mario Vaerewijck on drums. “Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version),” released as Suicide Commando marks its 40th anniversary, continues the project’s recent run of anniversary-focused releases alongside “Collective Suicide Vol. 1+2.”

items.body: German dark electro duo NER\OGRIS opened the digital pre-sale for their forthcoming album “Fame Fatale” on Bandcamp, timed to coincide with Bandcamp Friday, with several tracks available to stream immediately. The band’s webshop, offering the album on CD, vinyl and merchandise, is expected to go live the following week. Fame Fatale by NER\OGRIS NER\OGRIS features Kai Neugebauer and Amnistia vocalist Tino Claus. The duo are confirmed as special guests on Fïx8:Sëd8‘s RET(R)OUR 2026 tour, marking the tenth anniversary of Fïx8:Sëd8’s first mini-tour, running across the Czech Republic, Germany, Sweden and Belgium in October and November 2026. Jihad joins as an additional special guest on two German dates. NER\OGRIS and Fïx8:Sëd8 tour dates 17 October – Prague, Czech Republic – Futurum Music Bar 31 October – Münster, Germany – Sputnikhalle 6 November – Stockholm, Sweden – Nalen Klubb 7 November – Gothenburg, Sweden – Spike Brewery 14 November – Liège, Belgium – La Zone 20 November – Hannover, Germany – SubKultur (special guest: Jihad) 21 November – Freiberg, Germany – EAC Freiberg (special guest: Jihad) 27 November – Berlin, Germany – Urban Spree 28 November – Schmalkalden, Germany – Villa K About NER\OGRIS NER\OGRIS was formed in February 2022 by Kai Neugebauer and Tino Claus, who also performs as vocalist of Amnistia. The two met in 2014 and named the project by combining “nero,” for black, and “gris,” for grey. NER\OGRIS signed to Dependent Records and released the debut album “I Am the Shadow – I Am the Light” in February 2023, preceded by the video single “Deepest Fear.” The band followed with the mini-album “Silenci” in November 2025, released on CD with a 12″ vinyl edition arriving in January 2026. “Fame Fatale,” now in digital pre-sale, is the duo’s next full-length, arriving alongside their support slot on Fïx8:Sëd8’s RET(R)OUR 2026 tour.

items.body: CK 37, the Swedish electronic body music trio, releases the single “All Inclusive” on August 14, 2026, through Audite Records. Pre-orders opened on Bandcamp on August 7, 2026, ahead of the track’s arrival on major streaming platforms on its release date. All Inclusive by CK 37 CK 37’s ‘All Inclusive’ takes aim at package holidays “All Inclusive” follows CK 37’s debut album “Inget Hat” and a summer of touring across Sweden and Germany. The track turns to the theme of the all-inclusive package holiday, addressing sunbed culture, bar queues, water aerobics and standardized vacationing with humour. Musically, it carries the pounding rhythms and big hooks the band has built its sound on since its earliest singles. About CK 37 CK 37 are a Swedish electronic body music trio whose name derives from Centralkalkylator 37, the central flight computer built for the Saab 37 Viggen. The project mixes old-school EBM with electro and minimal synth. The trio issued their debut single “Gymsadist” in October 2024, followed by the Kraftwerk homage “Autobahn (Fan Fan Fan)” in March 2025 and the single “800º” in May 2025. Their debut album “Inget Hat” arrived on 9 January 2026 through Audite Records on orange clear vinyl and digital. Across June and July 2026 the band released seven remix EPs drawn from that album, gathered into the collection “Inget Hat (Remixer)”. The band toured Sweden and Germany over the summer before returning with “All Inclusive,” released August 14, 2026.

items.body: KMFDM released the single “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” on Metropolis Records on 7 August 2026. The single reworks the title track of the industrial rock band’s album “Enemy,” released in February 2026, and is streaming via ffm.to/mqxraqy and on Bandcamp. Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix) by KMFDM The remix comes from producer Matia Simovich, who records as Inhalt and owns Infinite Power Studios in Los Angeles. Simovich has previously worked as co-writer and/or producer with Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream, Boy Harsher, Nitzer Ebb, Patriarchy and Madeline Goldstein. “KMFDM were a teenage instruction manual on how to arrange a song and subvert the status quo, all packaged under an ultra heavy beat,” Simovich stated. On the remix itself, Simovich commented: “I spent a whirlwind week putting the original song to the dancefloor, aided by an amazing polyphonic modular synthesizer but mixing to analog tape. I hope this remix lands with KMFDM fans new and old. It’s part dubby in the ‘UAIOE’ way, part Zappa in the ‘MONEY’ way, but all KMFDM attitude under the INHALT lens.” The comparisons reference KMFDM’s 1989 album “UAIÖE” and 1992 album “Money.” “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” is Simovich’s second KMFDM rework. He previously remixed the album track “Yoü” as “Yoü (Inhalt Kunst ’93 Remix),” released in April 2026 and streaming at ffm.to/youmix. The “Enemy” album was previewed with the songs “Oubliette” and its title track as singles and received positive reviews on release. About KMFDM KMFDM began in Paris in 1984 as a performance art project between Sascha Konietzko and German multimedia artist Udo Sturm. Konietzko, joined by drummer En Esch and vocalist Raymond Watts, recorded the band’s earliest material in Germany before relocating to Chicago, where KMFDM signed to the industrial label Wax Trax! Records and built its reputation through the late 1980s and 1990s with albums including “UAIÖE” (1989) and “Money” (1992). Konietzko is the only member to appear on every KMFDM release. Vocalist Lucia Cifarelli, Konietzko’s wife, joined the band’s lineup around the turn of the 2000s, and KMFDM has released through Metropolis Records for its more recent output. The band’s current lineup features Konietzko, Cifarelli and drummer Andy Selway, with contributions from Tidor Nieddu and Annabella Konietzko – daughter of Sascha Konietzko and Lucia Cifarelli – on the “Enemy” album. “Enemy,” released in February 2026, was followed by the “Yoü (Inhalt Kunst ’93 Remix)” single in April 2026 and now by “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” in August 2026, both reworked by producer Matia Simovich (Inhalt).

items.body: Dark the Keeper (DTK), the dark ambient and industrial project of producer and musician Alexander Borsov, released the twelve-track album “Psychic Microbe” digitally on Aliens Production in August 2026. Psychic Microbe by Dark the Keeper “Psychic Microbe” contains “Soul Burn,” “Unbending Character,” “Dark Idea Generator,” “Soul Hunter,” “Engine of Hell,” “Labyrinth of Hell,” “Whisper of Shadows,” “Paranoid Delusions,” “Trap-Manipulation,” “Paraphrenia II,” “March of Immortality” and “Hidden Hatred.” Borsov wrote and produced the album under the Dark the Keeper name, designed its artwork and handled mastering himself. Aliens Production describes Borsov’s dark, hybrid signature style as manifesting in dense, complex compositions that blend cinematic sequences and industrial blocks with a combination of slow rhythms and analog loops, a description that applies to the layered, atmospheric approach carried through “Psychic Microbe.” About Dark the Keeper Dark the Keeper is one of the recording names used by producer and musician Alexander Borsov, who works across several projects and musical transformations within the dark ambient and industrial fields. As DTK, Borsov handles composition, production, mastering and design under a single artistic vision built on dense, cinematic arrangements combined with industrial textures, slow rhythms and analog loops. The project releases through Aliens Production, a Slovak dark electronics label active since 1997 whose roster includes dISHARMONY, Oxyd, Headdreamer, Fractal and Human Vault. “Psychic Microbe,” released digitally in August 2026, is Dark the Keeper’s latest full-length under the label.

items.body: Detroit industrial-punk duo Credit Card released the single “Love Crime” on August 6, 2026. The track is the second single from the band’s debut album, “Devil’s Night / Dead Internet,” a self-released, 12-track digital album due August 14, 2026 via Bandcamp. Credit Card is Shaun Hunter, who handles vocals, synth and noise, and Max Dameron, who supplies programming, synth and guitar. On “Love Crime,” the duo pair a hard-driving, mechanically programmed beat with distorted synths, noise and guitar under Hunter’s vocals. The song follows the band’s debut single “Harsh Times,” released July 15, 2026 and previously covered by Side-Line. Love Crime by Credit Card “Devil’s Night / Dead Internet” is available for pre-order on Bandcamp ahead of its August 14 release. The album runs 12 tracks: “cute.exe,” “This Is a Debt You Can Never Repay,” “RHCP Tattoo,” “Love Crime,” “Pure Mood,” “Mister Sophistication,” “Harsh Times,” “Lifestyle Creep,” “Vampire’s Kiss,” “I Thought You Said This Is Dust, Brother,” “Nero With Venus” and “Do What You Want.” No label is listed for the release; Credit Card has issued both singles independently through Bandcamp. No Discogs profile for the band could be located at the time of writing. About Credit Card Credit Card is a duo from Detroit, Michigan, formed by Shaun Hunter (vocals, synth, noise) and Max Dameron (programming, synth, guitar). The project built a following in Detroit through live shows built around strobe lighting and mosh pits. Its first physical release, a seven-inch single titled “(CC)” – a reference to the Germs – sold out at its release show. Credit Card released its debut single, “Harsh Times,” on July 15, 2026, self-released via Bandcamp. “Love Crime,” released August 6, 2026, followed as the second single from the band’s forthcoming debut album, “Devil’s Night / Dead Internet,” a 12-track digital release scheduled for August 14, 2026 via Bandcamp. No label has been announced for the release.

items.body: Minneapolis-based post-industrial artist EbE404 will release its third full-length album, “Cortisol,” on CD and digital August 21, 2026 via GIVE/TAKE. Pre-orders open August 7, 2026. The album comprises nine long-form drone, noise and power ambient pieces and follows the maxi-single “Flora,” due July 31, 2026 on the same label. ‘Cortisol’ unfolds across nine tracks “Cortisol” is described by GIVE/TAKE as a statement on the attention economy, built from reverb-soaked, multi-layered atmospheres and minimal rhythmic elements. EbE404 applies spatial mixing, interacting frequencies and phase manipulation across the record’s nine tracks. The label points to the project’s 2020 debut, “Tedium and Loss,” as a reference point for the album’s dark ambient tone. The label also states the release will not appear on Spotify, citing anti-AI marketing methods built around direct human sharing rather than algorithmic platforms. EbE404 describes the album directly: “This album is the sound of living through fascism, the worst people in the world, the execution of empathy, and a life being shaped by algorithms and a digital universe that is utterly detached from the real world – the inevitable result of The Attention Economy. Cortisol is the stress hormone, and this work traces the rise and fall of it as one meanders between virtual and structural nightmares while finding moments of distraction and respite. Feeling the unprecedented becoming normal and fighting to remain anchored in the real to avoid desensitization. Minneapolis has been a strange place to make art in this era, and this captures the horrors and hope of fighting back. This is for The Rebel Loons.” GIVE/TAKE lists reference points including Coil’s “Constant Shallowness Leads to Evil” era and Throbbing Gristle’s “Third Mind Movement” era. A Bandcamp listening party with EbE404 is set for release day, August 21, 2026 at 7 p.m. CST. About EbE404 EbE404 is a Minneapolis-based electronic project that keeps its members anonymous, working across post-industrial, dark ambient and IDM territory built around modular synthesis, Ableton Live sound design and field recordings. The project cites Coil, Nurse With Wound and Lustmord as reference points. EbE404 released its debut album, “Tedium and Loss,” on GIVE/TAKE on October 16, 2020. The second album, “Inrush,” followed on May 6, 2022; Side-Line spoke with EbE404 that year in a Click Interview, where the project described “Inrush” as a condensed 24-hour cycle exploring the patterns and routines of daily life. A remix album, “Ripple,” arrived August 19, 2022, followed by “Dark Ice Days” on July 21, 2023. “Cortisol,” set for August 21, 2026, arrives roughly three weeks after the maxi-single “Flora,” which previews the album with three versions of the track “Grass Time.” It is EbE404’s third full-length for GIVE/TAKE.

items.body: Belgian dark electro project Mildreda released a lyric video for “Silk Skin” on August 6, 2026, the latest advance single from the double album “Realities”, due August 28, 2026 on Dependent Records. “Silk Skin” opens the second disc of the release and follows earlier singles “End of the Line” and “Virtual Goddess”, the latter featuring Suicide Commando’s Johan Van Roy. ‘Silk Skin’: theme and production Mildreda mastermind Jan Dewulf wrote and produced “Silk Skin” around the tension between longing and retreat. “This track revolves around unspoken desires and the familiar, exhausting push and pull between longing and retreat,” Dewulf said. “I wanted to transform that tension into a ritual – a feverish invocation, a dance that binds, summons, and slowly pulls you under. Musically, the heavy bass was a happy accident in the studio, one that instantly revealed the direction that I needed to take. A relentless pulse rooted in EBM, and unmistakably Belgian at its sonic core.” Dewulf recorded, produced and mixed “Silk Skin” at Cyberflesh Loft in Ostend, with mastering by Pieter De Wagter at Equus in Vlezenbeek. The single has been cleared for immediate radio broadcast, and cover art and layout for “Realities” are by Henk Willems. About Mildreda Mildreda is the dark electro project of Belgian musician Jan Dewulf, who also records as Diskonnekted. Dewulf began Mildreda in the mid-1990s, drawn to the electronic body music of Belgian acts such as The Klinik, before setting the project aside to found Diskonnekted. He revived Mildreda in the 2010s, signing to Dependent Records and releasing “I Was Never Really There” in 2021 and the concept album “Blue-Devilled” in 2023. Christophe Salvatore plays live keyboards in the current line-up. The double album “Realities” follows “Blue-Devilled” as an 18-track, two-CD release on Dependent Records, featuring guest vocals from Suicide Commando‘s Johan Van Roy on “Virtual Goddess” and Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada on “Rückwärts”. “Silk Skin” is the album’s latest preview ahead of its August 28, 2026 release.

items.body: Industrial pop veteran Aesthetic Perfection released the single and video “Villain Era” on August 7, 2026 via Out Of Line Music, previewing the band’s next full-length album. The track combines danceable, upbeat industrial pop with a dark edge, built around the idea of embracing rather than resisting one’s darker impulses. ‘Villain Era’: lyrics and release context Lyrically, “Villain Era” traces a narrator’s slow surrender to a darker side of the self, with the line “I’m slipping away, my villain is taking over” marking a point of no return. The single follows Aesthetic Perfection’s appearance at Till Fest in Leipzig, where the band played both days of the festival alongside Till Lindemann and Ministry. The group has further festival dates confirmed at M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim and Summer Breeze Open Air, both in Germany, ahead of a headline European tour across the UK, France, Germany and Czechia in October and November 2026. Aesthetic Perfection has also been confirmed for AMPHI Festival 2027 in Cologne. About Aesthetic Perfection Aesthetic Perfection is an industrial pop project led by Los Angeles-born, Austria-based producer Daniel Graves, alongside Los Angeles native Constance Antoinette and New York-based drummer Joe Letz. Over a 25-year career, the band has blended industrial, pop and goth elements across seven full-length albums and numerous singles and music videos, building a loyal global fanbase and selling out headline tours across Europe and North America, including support tours with Till Lindemann. Aesthetic Perfection’s collaborators have included Sean Beavan, known for his work with Nine Inch Nails and Marilyn Manson, Jinxx of Black Veil Brides, and Rhys Fulber of Fear Factory, and the band’s music has featured in Netflix originals and on the “Underworld: Awakening” soundtrack. “Villain Era” offers a further taste of new material ahead of the band’s next full-length release, signed to Out Of Line Music.
